Mr. S. W. JACOBS (George Etienne Cartier) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 28 to amend the Railway Act, 1919.
He said: This bill is similar to one which I introduced into the House last year but which met with an untimely end in the Railway committee. I hope to have better luck with the bill this time. The bill seeks to amend the Railway Act to provide that a return ticket issued by any railway company between any two points in Canada shall be accepted by any other railway company whose line runs between the same termini.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

1.	Has the hounourable Minister of Agriculture or any other member of the government received any official confirmation of the recent Washington despatch intending that all contemplated instructions upon the export of Canadian potatoes into the United States after February 1, 1923, have been withdrawn?
2.	If so, will such be made public for the benefit of the Canadian potato growers who are much perplexed and alarmed at the prospect of being shut out of the United States market altogether as the imposition of the proposed instructions referred to would undoubtedly have resulted in?

The Federal Horticultural Board of the United States Department of Agriculture recently * passed an amendment to their regulations governing potato importations, to come into effect February 1, 1923. Under this amendment, shipments of Canadian potatoes could be imported only when accompanied by a certificate from an officer of the Canadian Department to the effect that they were free from injurious diseases or insect pests.
As it was at once apparent that considerable difficulty would be involved, and considerable expense incurred if the Canadian department were required to furnish this additional inspection service, an officer of the
department was sent to Washington to interview the Federal Horticultural Board, and endeavour to have the matter reconsidered. He received a sympathetic hearing, and the members of the board intimated that in view of the cordial relations that have existed between the Federal and United States departments in efforts to prevent the introduction into the continent of North America of plant diseases and insect pests from abroad, they would withdraw their action towards Canada in connection with this particular amendment to their regulations.
The following press notice has just been received from the official press service of the United States department:
U.S. Department of Agriculture, office of the Secretary.
Withdraws restrictions on import of potatoes from Canada and Bermuda
Washington, February 13: The United States Department of Agriculture to-day issued the following notice of the withdrawal of restrictions on the importation of potatoes from Canada and Bermuda other than such inspection as shall be deemed necessary from time to time:
Amendment No. 2 to regulations governing the importation of potatoes into the United States withdrawn.
Notice is hereby given of the withdrawal of amendment No. 2 revising the paragraph governing the entry of potatoes into the United States from Canada and Bermuda in regulation 7 of the regulations governing the importation of potatoes into the United States. This amendment was promulgated January 17, 1923, and was to become effective February 1st, 1923, and provided for official certification of the potatoes as to district of origin and as to freedom from injurious diseases and insect pests. The withdrawal of this amendment leaves without restriction the entry of potatoes from Canada and Bermuda other than such inspection as shall be deemed to be necessary from time to time to determine the freedom of such imports from injurious diseases and insect pests. The Federal Horticultural Board recommends this action after further consultation with the experts of the department and with the Dominion authorities, and in view of a general plan now under consideration to control under permit and inspection, the entry of all fruits and vegetables from foreign countries.
Henry C. Wallace,
Secretary of Agriculture.
This notice indicates that the entry of Canadian potatoes into the United States may be carried on just as in the past, so far as inspection is concerned, but shippers should certainly, in their own interests, avoid the shipment of potatoes hot of superior quality in every respect.

Mr. WILLIAM IRVINE (Calgary East) moved;
That, in the opinion of this House, a representative parliamentary committee should be appointed to investigate the basis, the function and the control of financial credit, and the relation of credit to the industrial problems.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this resolution asks for an investigation into the basis and function of credit, either by a parliamentary committee or by some other committee which parliament might see fit to appoint. The resolution calls for a parliamentary committee, but the main point before us is the consideration of the advisability of getting the information on the basis and function of credit and the relation

Credit and Industry
of credit to industry. It is my duty, then, to show the necessity for such information. Hon. members of the House will recall that last year on two occasions I laid the basis for this resolution,-in the debate in reply to the Speech from the Throne, and in the debate on the budget. I set forth what credit was; how it was controlled; its indispensability to modem society; how inflation and deflation is controlled by the banks; that the present industrial paralysis is due largely to a lack of purchasing power; that the development of our home market should be sought by increasing the purchasing power of the country. I showed further the relation of credit control to war, and indicated the danger of collapse of the present financial system; and also gave an analysis of substitute proposals by a number of students of finance.
I was rather interested, Mr. Speaker, last year, to observe the effect which my discussion of this question produced on some hon. members of the House, and particularly was I interested in the remarks which it called forth from the hon. member for Halifax (Mr. Maclean). I notice that the hon. gentleman is not in his seat at the moment, but on that occasion the discussion tempted him into an unusual outburst of humour. Either he did not think the subject as I presented it was worthy of serious consideration or he was not in a position to answer the argument. Be that as it may, he replied by indulging in sarcasm at my expense. He even went so far as to be willing to break the bonds of the Empire, to place upon my head a golden crown, if I could instruct people of Canada how to pay the national debt, or how to get rid of interest, and so forth. Now I notice by -a report in the daily press that the hon. member for Halifax is slated as the next Minister of Finance for this Dominion. If that is true I venture to say that this House and the people of Canada will require a better answer to the question of finance and credit from the hon. gentleman than the sarcasm which he gave to the House last year. I trust that to-day he will take the opportunity to go into the matter in greater detail and with more seriousness than he bestowed upon it on that occasion.
I want to point out that the contention of last year has been substantiated by financiers of world repute. I would mention first Col. Armstrong. In referring to the Cunliff committee that was appointed by the British government to make recommendations as to industry and finance shortly after the war, he points out:
It is now generally agreed that the policy of deflation which the government adopted in accordance with the
*10 j
recommendations of the Cunliff committee'has proceeded too far and produced results which were not anticipated at the time it was Instituted.
In that connection also I would refer the House to the utterances of Lord Milner, who happens to be himself a bank director in England. He refers to this question more from the point of view of labour, and goes on to show how labouring people were induced to increase production after the war. Their wages were cut -and deflation in finance was brought about, with the result that the storehouses of the nation were filled with goods. The people had no money with which to purchase these goods, and the inevitable results followed-unemployment. But more than that-Lord Milner says:
Labour is more and more inclined to question the competence of the bigwigs of industry and finance. There is a loss of confidence in the management.
Continuing he says:
For months and months after the close of the war he-the labour man-had it dinned into his ears that the world was suffering from a shortage of goods, and he was overwhelmed with exhortations to him and the men of his class not to spare themselves, but to work with intensified energy to make up the deficiency. That, he was vehemently assured, was their duty to their country and the world, and at the same time the one sure road to the improvement of their own condition. Such was the unanimous appeal made to him by all the highest authorities in the world of industry and finance. And he obeyed it to the best of his ability, but only to find, a year or two later, that the ware houses of his employers were choked with goods which they could not sell, and that his services were no longer required. And then, when, stung by disappointment, he began to probe for himself into the causes of this strange contradiction, he was told that there had unfortunately been a mistake, that the activity to which he had been so fervently exhorted to contribute was "feverish", that he ought to have known, we ought all to have known, that after the war there was bound to be a big slump, because "the pool of capital had been depleted" and w'e had no money for making things and nobody else had any money for buying them.
It would therefore seem that my contentions of last year were not matters for humour as the hon. member for Halifax seemed to think. Rather, these matters, have been taken very seriously indeed by some of the foremost financiers of the world. If generations of pyramiding debts and the control of credit by a select few financiers, with its inevitable under consumption and unemployment be made matters for mirth, then all I have to say is that some hon. members have a rather peculiar idea of what constitutes humour. Is the present situation as referred to by Lord Milner-and it is obvious in Canada, and, indeed, all over the world- is the present situation the best that the present financiers and their advocates, can give us. If so, I submit that these ad-
Credit and Industry

vocates ought to be willing to listen, to other people, however ignorant they may seem to be.
What, let us ask first, are the industrial conditions in Canada at the present time? In this regard I would refer in the first place, to the evidence that has been given in this House by the representatives of agriculture in the Dominion. Nobody will deny that their speeches have reflected the protest of the agricultural population against an industrial situation which is becoming intolerable. In this connection I would quote a very short extract from Dr. Henrik Shipstead, a senator from Minnesota who says:
The farmers of Minnesota left thousands of acres of potatoes in the fields to rot-thousands upon thousands of acres, and the country needing cheap food. They could not afford to dig them for there was no market for them-think of that, no market for them!
That is the situation in Canada to a large extent. There is no market for wheat-prices are low; there is no market for cattle-prices are below the margin where it is possible to raise cattle economically. So from the point of view of agriculture, the industrial situation in Canada is indeed very serious.
I would also refer to the business depression which set in shortly after the close of the war, and which still persists. It stands to reason that business must be depressed when there is no market for the farmers' produce and no employment for the working people; under such conditions business must of necessity be depressed. In this connection it is well to refer to the depletion of our population which is going on because of the economic conditions in agriculture, in industry and in business, and I could not do better than quote a short passage from an article from the pen of Mr. John A. Stevenson in MacLean's magazine. The heading of this article is: "Is Canada an Immigration Sieve?" I quote from it briefly:
From the Maritime provinces fifty families per week are said to be moving to the New England states, and at the other end of the country Col. W. B. Forster, of Vancouver, declares that the province has lost 177,000 people by emigration in the last decade, although the Vancouver Province challenges his figures.
But, perhaps the most deadly evidence of all comes from the customs returns, which show that in the year ending December 31, whereas the value of imports under the head of "settlers effects'' total $6,195,569, the parallel exports reached $7,832,052. This clear loss on the balance is a most disconcerting novelty.
But little further proof of the existence of a steady exodus is needed beyond the latest census figures. In 1911, the population was officially estimated at 7,206,463. In the succeeding decade, 1,975,000 people entered our gates, and the natural increment should normally have been 1,800,000. Making the fullest allowance for losses of the war, the census of 1921, if Canada had retained all her native-born increment and her immigrants, should
(Mr. Irvine.]	<§j
have reached a total of 10,500,000. But the actual figures, as given by the Bureau of Statistics, are 8,769,489.
So, it will be seen that the economic conditions which have been brought to the attention of this House by hon. members representing the agricultural industry, and also the statistics with regard to the exodus from Canada of our people, prove that our economic conditions are very serious.
Next, I would refer to unemployment, which is still a grave problem in Canada. To make that point clear, I will quote from a telegram just received:
I am acting on behalf of the unemployed of Halifax. There are fifteen hundred of them. This situation has been with us for the past two years. I have wired Prime Minister and Minister of Labour on the subject urging the government to open up public works or give a greater measure of relief on account of a long period. The situation is acute.
I have in my hand a copy of a resolution sent from Sydney Mines to the Prime Minister with regard to the same situation, stating that "two hundred and upwards have been out of employment and are now suffering on account of said unemployment." I mention those just because they are fresh in this morning. The situation throughout all Canada is similar, and I would refer hon. members to the statement which was given by the leader of the Labour party (Mr. Woodsworth) in this House on a previous occasion with regard to the unemployment situation.
These industrial conditions are not, as many people contend, caused by the war. Let me give the evidence in support of this contention. In the first place, we had similar conditions in 1914. We had similar unemployment, similar business depression, arising out of the same economic conditions, which are producing the industrial paralysis from which we are at present suffering. War could not have caused that-the war had not yet begun. Again, we are better equipped at this time for production, and increased production if required, than we were prior to the war. I pointed that out at some length in the debate on this question last session. I showed that during the war we had increased our productive facilities; that we had brought home our men from the front, thus having more people to work, and so forth. I showed that we were in a better position for production after the war than we were before. In view of this, there cannot be any claim that we ought to suffer for lack of goods. Moreover, it must be said that if the stock of consumable goods has been depleted in Canada owing to war activities-and let me add that that is the only sane reason why anybody in Canada should be lacking for anything of necessity-

Credit and Industry
would it not be natural that every man and woman in this country who can work, would be working overtime to make up the shortage? On the contrary, not only are we not working to make up the shortage, we are feeding our people by a dole system, municipal or provincial or Dominion doles as the case may be and keeping them in idleness. When that is the situation, who will argue that Canada is in need of producing more goods? No, the problem of production has been solved. What we are sticking at is distribution of the goods. When you stop distributing, naturally you block up the whole industrial machine and it stops. What we want is not more production; we can produce more very speedily. What we want is more distribution; and that leads us, as I shall show later, to a consideration of the purchasing power of the people.
But let me come to the next point. If there was a shortage, which there is not, that shortage could not be explained by saying that we lack raw material, for obviously, Canada, with her boasted natural resources, can supply us with all the raw material required for production. The present situation has not arisen through a lack of plant equipment, as I have demonstrated; it has not arisen through a lack of willing workers, for they are walking the streets now looking for work. It has arisen because of the shortage of a real demand owing to a lack of purchasing power. Let me illustrate this. In the city of Calgary we require a new post office, not a political post office, but a real post office. Political parties have, for some time, as an election talk, been promising to build a post office at Calgary. But let us leave this aside and point to the fact that we have the spot of ground on which we want to set the post office. We have in Calgary, or can secure, the material out of which the post office would have to be built. We have in Calgary the labour, walking the streets, doing nothing, looking for an opportunity to build the post office. We are renting from private institutions offices for public purposes to the extent of $50,000 yearly. We, therefore, need the post office; but although we have the place upon which the post office would rest very solidly, the material out of which to build it, the men doing nothing that want to go to work at building it, and the need which would save us $50,000 a year in rent alone, we cannot build the post office because, it is said: "We have no money." Let me give you a parallel illustration. I will take you out to a river bank and I will show you a tribe of Indians sitting on the river bank disconsolate and distressed. I approach them and I ask the chief: "What is the matter?"
"Oh," he says, "We cannot fish and we cannot hunt because we have no money." I say: "Man, you have lots of fishing tackle, and I see there are fish in the stream. You have lots of guns and ammunition, and I see there is plenty of game in the bush. Why do you not fish and hunt?" "Oh, yes," says the chief, with tears in his eyes; we have lots of fishing material and there are lots of fish; we have lots of ammunition and there is plenty of game; but, you know, we cannot fish and we cannot hunt because we have no money." We would promptly send that whole tribe to the asylum; but when we are sending that tribe to the asylum, let us all go along with them, because we are doing precisely the same thing in Canada as that hypothetical tribe of Indians would be doing by taking such a stupid attitude as that.
The present industrial situation, as I have briefly outlined it, marks the bankruptcy of statesmanship in Canada. With our natural resources tremendous in extent, with the need on the part of the people for goods, with the men walking the streets seeking work-we cannot give them, I say that situation is indeed ridiculous. In support of the contention that this condition is brought about through lack of purchasing power, let me quote a few brief extracts from others that may be taken as greater authorities than myself. Let me quote first from an article in the Manchester Guardian. This article has the significant heading, "A Year of Disastrous Plenty." Note that heading. The article says:
As we sing our psalms of thanksgiving for o.ie of the most bountiful fruit harvests within memory, that the great part of the harvest is rotting beneath the trees that bore it, and we add to our thanks a prayer for economic enlightenment:
It concludes " The fruit trade has met its Waterloo."
Here is. another short extract from the Bulletin of the International City Bank of New York:
It is however a familiar fact that the chief cause of depression during the past year was the unbalanced state of industry, great numbers of would-be customers being unable to buy freely because their own product did not give them the required purchasing power over other products held at a higher level of values.
To conclude the quotations on this point, I will refer to Mr. Babson on purchasing power. He says:
The purchasing power of the people is ultimately determined by the total payroll of the nation. No matter what one's attitude is on the matters of labour and capital, in the final analjrsis it must be realized that the spending power, the purchasing power of a nation, of a community, is merely the sum total of the payroll of that nation or community.
For this reason then, that the deflation practised in Canada and in all countries has

resulted in unemployment through the curtailing of the purchasing power of the people, I urge that the investigation of this matter should be taken up by a committee of this parliament to see how this condition has been brought about. Here is the opportunity, by developing a credit system that will increase the purchasing power of our people, and start industries, and keep our people busy, so that afterwards, if we have unemployment, it will not be forced unemployment, but will be because we have actually produced more than we can possibly consume. That would be a very excellent condition and much more healthy, economically considered, than the unemployment at the present time. I want, therefore, an investigation that will reveal why there is a lack of financial credit in Canada at the present time. That is a reasonable and modest request. If it can be shown there are sound reasons for the prevailing shortage in financial credit, then I and other members of the House will be content. Let us hold the investigation tMr. Irvine.]
and have the proof. Nothing short of the proof will satisfy us.
My next point is that Canada has to borrow money. We borrowed hundreds of millions last year. I do not know how much we shall have to borrow this year, but I know that the Dominion government alone has to pay an annual interest on our borrowings of $138,223,000. Now, we have some advocates of economy. Here is an excellent place to practise economy. Can we save the interest on $138,000,000 to the people of Canada? That would certainly be a worthy accomplishment and would be good economy. Have we the chance of practising economy in this way? We borrow a great deal of our money from the United States. In the process of borrowing we have to pay brokers high rates for handling our business. We have to pay high rates of interest to somebody for permitting us to use our own credit-it is a well-known fact that we cannot borrow from anybody unless we already have a basis of borrowing. If you go to a bank to borrow money, the banker will ask you what you have got, and when you have demonstrated that you have assets equal and more than equal to what you want to borrow, he will consider your loan; in other words, you can only borrow from the banker what you already have. If we go to the United States and tell them that we are bankrupt as a nation, that we have no natural resources, no industries, and that we are all dying, how much would we be able to borrow? Nothing. We can only borrow from the United States because we already have the credit which merits the loan which we solicit. If that be true, I want to know why Canada cannot use her own credit. Why should we have to go to Wall street to get permission to use what we already have? Is the credit of Canada which is good enough for the Wall street banker not good enough for the Canadian manufacturer or the Canadian banker? Is it not good enough for the Canadian farmers? On this ground also then, I want an investigation to show how it is that we are forced to go into a foreign country to borrow money, why we cannot use our own credit and escape the burden of interest, and at the same time increase the people's purchasing power and start all the industries of Canada?
Next, I want to show that credit is a social asset, and, being social in character, and of supreme importance to the life of the nation, it must not be allowed to be controlled by any clique, no matter how wise or efficient its members may be. I do not need to tell the House that one of the chief factors of any nation's credit is its consumers, for the con-

When I was interrupted, I was dealing with the point that credit is a social asset, that the consumer is one -of the main factors of a nation, and that, every person being a consumer, credit was necessarily of a social character. If that is so then it is surely a dangerous thing to permit a few monopolists to control social credit. Credit is the lifeblood of industry; and we want an investigation to show who are the individuals that control the flow of the lifeblood of Canadian industry, and to find out if there be any possible way by which society can control the system. If there be then we must ascertain what is necessary to be done. And this investigation would serve to throw light upon this question.
My next point is that those who control the finances of any country control the government and, as well, the policy of industry. It must be clear to any hon. member who gives the matter a moment's consideration that a government that must borrow $100,000,000 or $200,000,000 or more from financiers cannot be absolutely independent of those financiers. When a government has already given them carte blanche with regard to the credit of the country, and given them a ten-year right to the use of it, then that government must come cap in hand to those financiers, the

government already having given away its own power. In support of this contention, which I cannot take the time to develop as fully as I should like, let me point to the situation in Alberta at the present time. We have in that province a Farmers' government, so-called, and we have had ap investigation by a royal commission into the banking conditions there. Simply because of that circumstance, we find that the financiers are taking a very hostile attitude. In a recent issue of the Calgary Daily Herald you will find a very interesting editorial on this point. The Herald declares that the Alberta government and the critics of finance in that province had better be careful because the financiers might take umbrage, and that if they did they could, if they so choose, shut oS the credit of the whole province. Now, that is proof, at least to some extent, that financiers may, and very likely do, control governments. It must be just as evident that he who controls finance controls the policy of industry. He who has the right to say whether a loan shall or shall not be secured, says, in very many instances, what sort of industry shall be established, and what sort shall not be allowed. Let me cite an illustration, the supposed case of a farmer and a moving picture showman going to a banker each soliciting the loan of, say, $1,000. In reply to the question concerning his assets, the farmer tells the banker that he has a mortgage on his farm already, in fact, two or three; that his wheat crop has been a failure; that he finds himself with a large quantity of stock, for which there is no market and for which he has no feed. However, if he could borrow $1,000 and secure feed to keep his cattle over the winter he might possibly come out all right the next year. That is his story. Then the banker turns to the other man and asks for his story. This man says he is going to establish a picture show in the town. He has rented such-and-such a building and wants to install the necessary machinery. He requires enough money to pay his help for the first month perhaps; and as regards the question of assets, he says he has a fine line of films which have been popular everywhere else and which he knows the people of this town will like. His patrons are in the community and he knows that they will come to see his pictures. He will make so much per night or per week and, he can give a reasonable promise that in a given time the money will be paid back. Well, the banker has nothing to do but to choose in favour of the picture showman. The banker is handling money that must make more money and he cannot lend to the farmer because he has no assurance that the

cattle market will improve or that the farmer will be able to pay back the amount lent him. And so the banker, without designing it, decides that instead of building up a cattle industry we shall build up a picture show business. I am not speaking against the picture show business; it is all right-but we shall not live very long on picture shows. We must first of all establish the basic industries that supply the necessities of life, and whatever is in the nature of a luxury can come later. From that illustration it will be seen that the man who controls the finance of a country controls also the policy of its industry. I therefore urge an inquiry into credit control. I want an investigation to see how it is that banks do control credit, and to see why we should continue to give carte blanche to a number of gentlemen to do what they please with Canada's credit.
Next let me show briefly that money is not performing its proper function in society. Normally the function that it should perform industrially would be analogous to that which the blood performs in its circulation through our bodies. The discovery of the circulation of the blood was of great moment to a proper understanding of the control of our bodily health. The discovery of the circulation of money as the life blood of industry to-day is a discovery of equally great importance to economics. One of the symptoms of a defective circulation of the blood in the body is cold feet, and I think perhaps we are suffering from that trouble to some extent to-day. Cold feet is something like greatness: Some are born with cold feet, some acquire cold feet, and some have cold feet thrust upon them. I do not know whether the present administration has been born with cold feet, or has acquired them, or has had cold feet thrust upon it. Nor do I know whether our present industrial monopolists have been born with that affliction or whether the financial situation has developed it in them, but the fact is that they have cold feet to-day. We need an investigation, then, to find out how it is that the circulation of finance is being arrested.
What is Canada suffering from at the present time? Is it fatty degeneration of the heart, or is it arterio-sclerosis that is impeding the circulation of finance? Whatever the disease, it is gnawing at the vitals of Canada, and this arrested circulation is making serious inroads upon the economic fife of the nation. Therefore, if we are to effect a cure we must have the necessary information on which to act.
Perhaps I can illustrate this from another point of view. The lack of purchasing power

is somewhat akin to the lack of electric power in a street railway system. Purchasing power makes the wheels go round in the industrial system, just as the electric current makes the wheels turn in a street car system. For want of the necessary electric power the most skilled workmen provided with the very best equipment are powerless to function. We have no shortage of plant or equipment in our industrial system, for during the war years great factories were equipped with the most modern machinery. Neither is there any lack of skilled operators, as I have already shown. But our industrial plants are standing idle and our operatives are unemployed periodically because something called "contraction of credit" cuts off the supply of currency. Now, surely the community should do something more than wTait around at street comers and starve during these interruptions until the "current" comes on again. What is the matter with our industrial system that it is not running? Has something happened to the machinery? Is there power enough? What is the matter? We want an investigation in order that we may find out where the trouble lies.
Now, in connection with the function of money, in our economic system, let me quote Delmar. He says:
When the principles that underlie it are thoroughly understood, money is perhaps the mightiest engine to which man can lend an intelligent guidance. Unheard, unfelt, unseen, it has the power so to distribute the burdens, gratifications and opportunities of life that each individual shall enjoy that share of them to which his merits or good fortune may entitle him or contrariwise to dispense them with bo partial a hand as to violate every principle of justice and perpetuate a succession uf social slaveries to the end of time.
What, then, is this thing that has so much power? Why was it invented? What function did it originally perform? Why and how did banks arise and get control? Let me go back for a minute or two to the origin of money. We find early society doing its trading in commodities-they exchanged real goods for real goods. But by and by, as social integration went on, this was found too cumbersome a method. For instance, supposing one of the hon. members of the Farmer party in this House wanted to go to New York for a trip, and his only wealth consisted of cattle. We will suppose he has a lot of steers, but there is no market for them, so he takes them down to New York, paying the freight charges with a certain number of them, also his railway fare and his hotel expenses. When he wants to go to a picture show he slices off a hind quarter and passes it through the ticket wicket. Such would be the cumbersome process if there was no money in use; in a word, it would be impossible under present day conditions, to do any trading without a medium of exchange. It is easily conceivable how necessary it was for our early ancestors to invent some means to facilitate business. They invented money. Sometimes it was made out of little pieces of wood, at other times of leather, skins, iron, brass, copper, until finally it reached its present form-paper. Anything will do for money as long as we give it legal sanction. But the point is that money is a shadow of the reality; that is, its real meaning and its function is to facilitate business, because, as I have pointed out, it is easier to take the shadow of a carload of steers to New York than the steers themselves.
But how did the shadow become a reality? It is easy for us to see how subsequent generations would lose the meaning of the function of money, and they would discover that whoever possessed money could do whatever he wanted. If he needed potatoes he could buy them with money, and would not need to raise them, and so on with other commodities. So, gradually people began to acquire money for the power it gave them; they began to hoard it; and eventually to guard against robbers it was found necessary to have strongboxes in which to keep their money and to appoint keepers to guard their boxes. By and by those strong-box keepers began to develop a notion of becoming bankers. One morning when one of these keepers was guarding a strong-box a sad looking farmer came along, and on being asked why he looked so downcast he exclaimed that he had his land all ready for crops but was without money to buy the necessary seed. Immediately the strong-box keeper, the embryo banker, conceived the brilliant idea of lending some of the money confided to his keeping to the farmer, who could pay him back the .principal with interest in the fall when he had harvested his crops. But then he was assailed by the doubt: Supposing I lend Jones' money to this farmer and Jones wants it in the meantime, what shall I do? He soon settled this difficulty by recollecting that he could satisfy Jones by paying him out of Smith's money. So he took the chance, made the loan to the farmer, and everything worked out so well that after a time instead of continuing as a strong-box keeper and paid for his sendees as such, he made an offer to pay hoarders interest on any money they would deposit with him. And lo and behold! all the old socks were turned inside out, the hoarders of money flocked to him, and he very soon was in control of 'the whole financial situation. That is how the bankers got their power.

That is what banks came for: first of all to guard money, and then later to control it. It is the function of money, as I have pointed out, to facilitate trade, and as I have shown money is the shadow of the reality.
I understand that the Bank Act will come up for revision this session. Once that is done, ten years more will elapse before we shall be in a position to discuss this financial question with any hope of having alterations made. It is very important, therefore, that we should get more information. Indeed, I doubt whether anyone in this House outside of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) himself and the late Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) really understands the present system of finance. Last year some hon. members objected to the new proposals of Major Douglas then put forward on the ground that they did not understand them; but those hoq. gentlemen do not understand the system that is in vogue now. I say we do not understand it, but we are going to revise and confirm an act that passes all financial and credit power into the hands of a few men for ten years. I submit that in view of the complex nature of this subject it is imperatively necessary that we should have more information in regard to it before we are called upon to vote on the Bank Act. If we do not, what will happen? The experts of the banks on the committee dealing with the bill will tell us what kind of bill they want, and we shall not be in a position to challenge them; their information will be expert information and the result will be that we shall have a banking act for bankers instead of a banldng act that will secure a free flow of the life blood of industry through Canada for the next ten years. For this, another reason, Mr. Speaker, I urge the necessity of an investigation into the subject matter of the resolution.
Moreover, the banking system, the finance system, of the world is in real danger of collapse. We have continued to pyramid our debts, and the pyramid has been inverted; it is standing on its apex, and we are building out and out to such an extent that if we keep on the whole thing will ultimately collapse around us. To change the illustration, let us imagine that a snake starts to eat its own tail. It keeps on eating and eating and by and by it comes to the back of its neck and can go no further. The financial system of the world is just about in that position now. One of the expert students of this subject whom I interviewed in London last summer told me that the system could not possibly go on longer than 1925, and he based his prophecy on the ratio of average overhead charges in

the great staple industries to the direct labour charges involved in connection with those industries. So there is a danger to civilization in this connection. If hon. members of this House found it necessary to put up at a hotel that was not fireproof, they would be pardoned for looking around for the fire escape. There is, I say, this possibility of catastrophe in the present world situation, and I want to know where the fire escape is. I want to know what this government will do in the event of the financial system of the world collapsing through the present invasion of the Ruhr by France. Indeed, that is a danger that the Prime Minister of England feared when he dissociated himself from the action of the Premier of France; that is what is feared by all students of finance. What will our government do in that event? Shall we not have an investigation into this matter so that we may know what course to pursue in the case of a collapse taking place?
We need a fundamental change in our banking system. When our Bank Act comes up for revision I shall not be interested in crossing its t's and dotting its i's, I do not think we can get much improvement from that. Indeed, the present Bank Act is a good act; it has been said that it is a good measure-for the bankers. It is one of the best acts in North America, or in the civilized world for that matter, for the bankers; and we might make it a little better for them by tinkering with it-I am not sure. At any rate, that is all I expect out of the procedure involved in a revision of the present act. Shall we not now take a new step; is there a chance of a fundamental change which will give us greater circulation of currency, which will stir up our industries, increase our home markets, solve the problem of distribution, prevent the paying of huge sums of interest?
There is a demand among the people for such information as this resolution seeks to obtain. Even the Liberal Association of Vancouver passed a fairly strong resolution demanding certain investigations and asking for changes in conection with the banking system of this country. The organized farmers and the organized labour people of this country have made similar demands. For the reasons I have given, therefore, I urge the adoption of this resolution in order that we may get the information that is so badly needed and that is so necessary before we can deal properly with any present or proposed banking legislation.
Mr. HENRY E. SPENCER (Battle River): Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to this resolu-

tion, I wish to say that it deals with one of the most important subjects that has come before this House. The hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Irvine) has stated the amount of interest that this country has to pay annually,-$138,223,000. It is interesting to note how our forefathers tried for many generations to get away from this tax. I might mention that King Alfred, about the year 900 A.D., forfeited goods of moneylenders, for usury. Edward the Confessor banished them from England. Henry II claimed usurers' property at death. Richard I and John punished them. Edward III made it a capital crime. Henry VIII allowed money to be loaned, and Elizabeth allowed a modified interest to be charged. For generations there was an effort to get away from the charge which to-day is piling up debts the world over. Efforts have been made from time to time to issue credit without this charge being attached to it. I am going to direct attention to two cases, one of which was referred to last year in a speech delivered by the member for Calgary East (Mr. Irvine) which will be found on page 2505 of Hansard. "Market- House Notes" were issued on the authority of Governor de L'Isle Brock of Guernsey, on the credit of the community, and no interest was charged. In the other case, in 1862, the American people had gone through a very expensive war and they needed a great . deal of money to pay their soldiers and sailors, and to purchase foodstuffs. It was decided, therefore, to issue what were known as greenbacks, and practically $450,000,000 were issued. In case hon. members of the House are not fully aware of the nature of the greenback, I wish to recite what one is. I quote from a former Secretary of the United States Treasury, Mr. Salmon P. Chase, who says:
What is a greenback? Did you ever think what it was? Why it is simply the credit of this great American people put into the form of money to circulate among the very people whose credit makes it good. When I was secretary' of the treasury, the question arose, how should these vast armies and navies be supplied, how should the boys be fed in the field, the sailors in ships, and provision made for their support and clothing, food and transportation? I found the banks of the country had suspended specie payment. What was I to do? The banks wanted me to borrow their credit. They did not pay me gold or propose to pay any themselves, but they wanted me to borrow their notes. I said "No, gentlemen, this great American people is worth all of you put together. I will take the credit of the people and cut it up in the form of little bits of paper and we will circulate that paper." This is the true idea of the greenback. It is the credit and property of the American people.
I do not wish the House to think for a minute that I am advocating the use of paper money without taking care of price regulation.
We have always to guard against the unnatural inflation, but it is worthy of note that the great American people after going through their severe struggle saw fit to make use of their own credit without charge. In our own case we did not do anything of the sort. After our great struggle we saw fit to borrow money on which we shall be paying a tax for generations to come to those who have loaned us the money, which we borrowed on our own credit.
Referring further to the issue of paper money in the United States, it was only natural that those who made their living by making loans or giving credit to individuals or the nation should fight such an innovation as this, and they kept up a running fight along the following lines. In 1877 a circular was issued by the authority of the Associated Bank of New York, Philadelphia and Boston, signed by one James Buell, Secretary, who issued it from 247 Broadway. I am quoting now from information given by Senator C. A. Lindbergh of the United States. This circular was sent to the Bankers in all the States and read:
Dear Sir,-It is advisable to do all in your power to sustain such prominent daily and weekly newspapers, especially the agricultural and religious press, as will oppose the greenback issue of paper money, and that you also withhold patronage from all applicants who are not willing to oppose the government issue of money. Let government issue the coin and the banks issue the paper money of the country, then we can better protect each other. To repeal the Act creating bank notes, or to restore to (circulation the government issue of money, will be to provide the people with money, and will therefore, seriously affect our individual profits as bankers and lenders. See your Congressman at once and engage him to support our interests that we may control legislation.
That, I must admit, is rather an interesting letter to obtain, and I think it is of particular interest at this time because we shall no doubt find that those who have the privilege of the control of credit in this country will, as efforts are made to take away that privilege, put forward similar propaganda.
One hardly realizes the power of what is known as interest. It is hard to believe that one dollar, at ten per cent compound interest will amount in a hundred years to the huge sum of $13,809.
During last session the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) came down to this House and informed the members that he had [DOT] been fortunate in floating a loan in New York to the amount of $100,000,000, at five per cent, for thirty years, and most of the hon. members applauded that statement. They applauded, I suppose, because they realized that Canada's name was so good that they were able to raise that loan in another country, but how
