many members realized that when the people of Canada meet that note, when it comes due in thirty years' time, they will have to pay back not only the $100,000,000, but the sum of $150,000,000 besides on account of interest. Study for a moment what this means in certain parts of Canada where high interest rates are being charged; I refer particularly to the western provinces. Interest is high there, and I have not the slightest hesitation in saying that when you consider the short term for which the loans are issued and the high rate of interest that is charged and compounded, the interest rate will easily equal ten per cent. Imagine, therefore, that for every hundred million dollars that are borrowed by the farmers of western Canada-on their own credit, mind you-when they come to pay that back in thirty years' time-if the renewal loan runs that long-they will pay no less a sum than $400,000,000. These figures, I think, are staggering.
As time has gone on, those who have controlled the money system of the country have gradually strengthened their hold, have organized themselves stronger and stronger until to-day we find that only a few men control the destinies of this country through finance. Going back just as far as 1904 I find that we had then thirty-four banks with some 1,100 branches, and in 1920 these banks had been reduced to eighteen with nearly 5,000 branches, and now as you well know, the number of banks is down to seventeen. One weakness in our present system appears to be that the banks are trying to carry on the business of this country on too little paid-up capital. In 1904 I notice that the relation of paid-up capital to assets equalled 11 per cent, but sixteen years afterwards it was only four per cent. It appears to me that the banks are trying to handle the country's business on too small a capital.
Credit when all is said and done is a community thing, but under the control we have at the present time, the credit of the country is entirely at the mercy of seventeen institutions. I would like to quote from a statement made by a banker of twenty years' standing. The figures are rather staggering. A layman, when he first comes across this, can hardly believe it is true. He says:
Banks are quasi-public institutions. The public must use them as thej' constitute a monopoly. These joint stock companies have invested of their own money [DOT] $129,000,000 and have accumulated from profits $135,000,000. Therefore, they have $264,000,000 of their own money in the business. This amount would not equal loans outside of Canada, which on June 30, 1921, were $321,000,000. Total assets on the same date were $2,879,000,000. All but $264,000,000 was the people's money. In other words the public has ten times as much interest in the banking business of our country as 
the shareholders of the banks and all the money is being controlled by eighteen groups of men. Over half of it is controlled by four groups. Two-thirds is controlled by seven banks. Seven men actually control over seventy per cent of the savings of nearly nine million people by the operation of seven machines, which gather their savings from towns, villages and hamlets, consolidating them in seven depositories, and then the seven men have the power to place this huge sum wherever it may suit them. '
I would like to quote a few words by Sir Edmund Walker, who, in speaking to the shareholders of the Bank of Commerce, on January 13, 1920, said:
We cannot adjust prices without also bringing about a contraction in the volume of paper money and other instruments of credit, and so far as it is possible to enforce contraction without interfering with the production of what is really necessary, the reduction of prices will be facilitated.
This is the way in which it was facilitated. In October, 1920, circulation amounted to $249,000,000. In three months this was reduced by $43,000,000, and by June 30, 1921, the banks had taken another $10,000,000 out of circulation. Had the decrease in circulation been less rapid, the results would not have been so disastrous. The sudden deflation was certainly appalling.
Banking monopoly naturally leads to industrial monopoly, and this reminds me, Mr. Speaker, of a very interesting debate which was held in this House last session and which you will find, in part, on page 1087 in Hansard. In reference to the debate on interlocking directorates, we had these astounding figures given us. We found that in one case fifteen men with interlocking directorates, with sixteen corporations, controlled a capital of no less than $4,285,000,000. To quote a few more figures along the same line, I should like to refer to the answer to a question which I put on the order paper during last session. The answer gave me the number of people, plus corporations, paying income tax as being 194,257. This, comparatively speaking, small number control an aggregate wealth of no less than $912,410,428. I cannot help, after quoting these few figures, but beg leave to draw your attention to how very closely a prophecy of the great President Lincoln has come true. President Lincoln, in his second letter to Congress, made this statement:
In my present position I could scarcely be justified were I to omit raising a warning voice against the approach of returning despotism. It is the effort to place capital above labour in the structure of the
government.
As a result of the war corporations have been enthroned, and an era of corruption in high places will follow, and the money power of the country will endeavour to prolong its reign by working upon the prejudices of the people until all wealth is aggregated in a few hands and the Republic is destroyed. I feel at this moment more anxiety for the safety of my

country than ever before, even in the midst of the war. God grant that my suspicions may prove groundless;
What are conditions in Canada at the present- time? We all admit that we have one of the finest countries in the world; that as an agricultural country, Canada takes a great deal of beating. We all admit that we can grow the finest grain and raise the best of stock. We all admit the vast potential wealth which we have in our minerals. We have a people with energy, perseverance and initiative second to none. We have huge manufacturing plants which have been bolstered up in legislative ways through a protective tariff. But, because of the large quantities we are turning out from our factories not being able to find a market,-under the present system,-in our own country, we are looking for a market abroad. But what is the present state of affairs? Our basic industry is in such a disastrous state that, with all the encouragement that people get to go on to the land, there is a steady drift going from the rural districts. An hon. member from this side of the House stated the other day that 113 people had left his little local town. Another one stated that fourteen families had left his particular district, and that not a single family had taken their place. This seems difficult to understand, when we consider the fact that in western Canada we have taken quantities of international prizes in the matter of grain and stock. The reason for this is not that the country is no good; it is not that the people are no good. The present state of affairs must be due to some other reason. We find Premier Bracken of Manitoba, stating the other day that in that province they have in arrears of taxes no less than $14,000,000, and this after a 'very successful crop. Word comes from Alberta that out of 80,000 farmers, 20,000 are insolvent, and I am told by members of this House that Saskatchewan is in a like plight. I do not know conditions so well in the East. We have been informed, during this session, of the large number of unemployed still in Canada, and one feels inclined to ask the reason why? It is just possible that we find one reason in the fact that we are carrying such a colossal debt. I found it rather interesting the other day to look up the indebtedness which the United States had when they had a population of some 30,000,000. If we compare that with our own nearly 9,000,000 people, and our national debt of some $2,500,000,000, we find that the United States, in the year 1860, with a population of 30,000,000, had a debt of only $65,000,000. Otherwise Canada, with one-third the population, has not less than thirty-eight times as much debt. That
Credit and Industry
may be one of the reasons why conditions are bad in Canada. We are informed in the address by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Irvine) that the total production of this country was no less than $6,000,000,000 and the total consumption was some $2,000,000,000. These figures are confirmed by the Dominion Statistician. In the ordinary walks of life anyone would think they were very well off if they only spent one-third of their income, but Canada seems to be the reverse. Quoting again from the prominent banker in Canada, he says:
Some people find it too easy to blame the war for all conditions, whereas the facts are that the banks could tell, if they would, that in some directions matters bad assumed a very serious aspect, and a crisis which many expected was avoided by the conflict.
We all recognize something is wrong. Each member, in any part of the House, has his own opinion as to what should be done, and although we differ, in our opinions, there is no need for any enmity to be shown between any members, because I believe every member in this House is actuated by the very highest motives in bringing forward what he considers the best suggestions for a way out of this dilemma. The orthodox remedies for this condition are the three following: immi- , gration, greater production and foreign markets. We have seen only too recently from various speakers that immigration has not increased population because of the emigration. We are not able to keep up our population. The matter of greater production is a false cry. All industrial countries have solved that problem long ago. It is not a question of greater production. It is a question of transportation and consumption. Look after the consumer and the producer will look after himself. As far as the foreign market goes, we have to realize that our foreign markets are the other people's home markets and their foreign markets are often our home markets.	It is not a matter of
finding foreign markets, but a matter of giving the people a purchasing power. All countries in my humble opinion should try and provide for their own needs first. How can a country buy foreign goods, if they cannot buy their own? As a proof that the question of production has been solved long ago, I might state that a fact has been mentioned by various eminent men, that the United States alone, if working at one hundred per cent capacity, could supply the needs of the whole world. The economists of Great Britain have often stated that ten per cent of the population of great Britain could supply her needs, if working at one hundred per cent efficiency. It is interest-

come directly from those conditions and have for many years been subject to them. We believe the statements we make are absolutely true, for they are borne out by the facts as we know them where we live, and consequently we would be derelict in our duty if we did not try to lay before the House the true facts regarding a large and important part of Canada. I believe that one of the most unfortunate conditions in this House is that we know so little concerning one another. In the West we know little about the people in the East, we know little about those who are engaged in farm and industrial activities, and they know about as little regarding ourselves. If we could have a true picture drawn of conditions in every part of the country, drawn by those who live there, I believe we could understand those various conditions and deal intelligently with them, and in that way discharge a very important function of parliament. I believe that the fuller and truer knowledge would lead to a greater sympathy, not only of industrial and commercial men for farmers, but of farmers for industrial and commercial men, and of farmers in one line of agriculture with farmers in other lines. From that greater sympathy might spring a spirit of co-operation without which we cannot hope that Canada ever will become the country she should become with her great natural endowments. With that end in view I should like to portray credit conditions as I have seen them in western Canada.
We have spoken in this House of the excessive cost of production being one of what we might term the greatest menaces with which agriculture is faced to-day, due to the fact that we have to sell our products in competition with the world, and that our whole salvation lies in lowering this excessive cost, a very important element of which at the present time is the cost of the credit we have to use in production. There are other elements which will have to be treated in due time. Throughout my district, perhaps one of the best in Alberta, we have suffered least from depression, from the very fact that long before the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) took office we followed his advice and adopted mixed farming, thus escaping those periods of deflation and expansion to which our wheat growing districts have been subject. We have been producing various products that we could sell every year, and therefore conditions there are not so deplorable as they are in some other parts. But even, there we find the debt of our farm-. ers has grown to very large proportions.
It may be said, and I think with justice, that the farmers themselves are to a large

extent responsible for that condition. I am not going to shirk that question. We have been through the optimistic boom years which preceded the post-war deflation, and naturally we were tempted into extravagant expenditures. But what other industries were exempt? We were tempted perhaps to buy beyond our means, as were those engaged in other industries. But the fact remains that we now have to bear the burden of that debt. In spite of what has been said there are very few farmers throughout the country who wish to shirk the responsibility of paying their just debts; but unfortunately there are some who feel that no matter how prosperous conditions may become again they will never be able to pay off their indebtedness. Tied hand and foot as they are financially, no matter whether their unfortunate condition be attributable to their own fault or to circumstances over which they have no control, when they fail to see the slightest gleam of hope in the future and are inclined to leave the country which they feel has not been just to them, we cannot altogether blame them. But the great majority of our farmers have sufficient faith in the productive ability of our country that, given a fair chance, they are determined to pay their debts. The question is, can they do it? And that brings me to my next point.
As I have stated, one of the main reasons for our excessive cost of production is our over-burden of debt. But is there any way of getting out of debt? I believe it is well worth the time of this House to consider if there is not some better method of financing our agriculturists and so enable them to carry on and produce. This is not only a plea for our farmers, it is a plea for the whole country, for I believe that our people are gradually beginning to realize that upon agriculture our national prosperity depends to a large extent. Recently I read a very well written paragraph in a book entitled "The Federal Farm Loan System in Operation". It is the work of Mr. A. C. Wiprud, and he epitomizes my argument so much better than I can hope to do it myself that I shall quote his words. He says:
The present importance of agriculture to civilization lies in the number of people it supports; its ultimate importance lies in the fact that it must continue to provide supplies for an ever-increasing population. The problems of our agricultural industry concern every member of society, and it behooves us to give them our earnest consideration.
It is from that point of view I desire to speak of the problem as a national problem. Since I came to this country thirty years ago as a boy from the Old Land and since becoming a member of this House, it has been my ex-

Credit and Industry
perience that agriculture has been largely-neglected. I am not blaming hon. gentlemen over much for that neglect, for the importance of agriculture has never been sufficiently realized, and it is only of late years since our economic foundation has begun to crumble that the secondary industries based on that foundation are becoming aware of their danger and of the intimate connection that exists, and must exist, between those industries. We have gone on year by year building up the superstructure of our industrial life by taking stone after stone from the foundation, until now our tall chimneys are beginning to rock and it is realized that if the foundation fails the superstructure must fail too. This neglect has not been confined to our own country. Let me just read what Mr. McAdoo says-and I think he will be recognized as a fairly good financial authority throughout this or any other country. He says:
It is a strange thing that throughout American history so little constructive and comprehensive work has been done to conserve the agricultural industry of the country. This industry is absolutely vital to the existence and prosperity of the people. Farmers as a class-
Mark this, because he expresses my thought in far better words than I myself can command.
-do not want superior advantages or benefits conferred upon them by legislation. They do want equal opportunity, and to get that equal opportunity they must have sufficient credit facilities at all times, and they must be available to them on as reasonable terms and at as low rates of interest as are allowed to our business men and manufacturers, due regard being had, of course, to the security offered and to the conditions applicable to each. In other words, agricultural credit should be as available as commercial credit, and upon equally favourable terms all things considered.
Now, I am speaking very briefly, because 1 recognize that the subject may become wearisome to some hon. members, and I realize also that time is passing. However, I will endeavour to show why the present. system has not been thoroughly satisfactory from the point of view of agriculture. You will understand that I am hot at this time attacking our present banking system, because I have not in my own mind a satisfactory system which can take its place. That is one point upon which I wish to have additional information, and it is another reason for the formation of a committee of inquiry. I do not believe, however, that we can have a system which will be not antagonistic but supplementary to our present banking system and will make it more adequate to agricultural needs.
What are the facts? The facts are-and 1 think I am stating them fairly-that owing to the nature of the funds at the disposal of our banks, funds which are liable to be called upon at almost a moment's notice, they cannot and
should not, in justice to their depositors, let any large portion of those funds out on any long-term credits. I think that can be taken as a statement of incontrovertible fact. But due to the nature of agriculture, due to. the fact that the turnover of the farmer is very slow, short-term credits are not suitable to his purposes. When the farmer borrows money on what may be a twelve months turnover in the case of grain or a three years turnover in the case of cattle, a loan for a period of three months is useless unless it is renewed from time to time, with consequent accumulation of interest. Now, that is the unsatisfactory part. Any farmer whose business is on a proper basis is willing to pay fair interest on proper terms for the credit he receives-credit which at the present time is simply the savings of the people. But the banks, I contend, are not in a position under their present system to extend credit on such terms that it is of value to us. It is a most peculiar thing that when one thinks along certain lines he almost invariably finds that someone else has also been thinking along that line and has expressed the view more concisely and in better language than you can yourself. This is what the authority that I have been quoting says on this subject:
In considering what constitutes the source of money supply, we should, of course, direct our attention to the commercial banks, for it is to them that a large part of the money of the nation is intrusted. The cash deposits which they receive, and which are the basis of their loans, they must at all times be prepared to restore either on demand or within a comparatively short time. For this reason they cannot properly invest m other than short-term mortgages or thirty to ninety days personal credits. In other words, deposits must be invested so that a steady stream of payments is flowing into the banks, giving them a chance to expand or contract their loans in response to the rise and fall in the supply of deposits.
In ordinary commerce, as I understand it- and I admit that my knowledge is limited-the turnover is comparatively rapid, and a credit of from three to six months is usually sufficient to cover ordinary commercial transactions. But that is not the case with agriculture, because the present financial system has failed as a system of credit so far as its application to agriculture is concerned. This situation has been recognized, I think, in all civilized countries. It was recognized in the United States; it has been recognized in Europe.
I am not going to speak of Europe, because the conditions of farming there are not applicable to our conditions here. A different style of farming is carried on; the sizes of the farms are different; there are different marketing conditions, different transportation problems-everything is different. But I think it is fair to regard as analogous the con-

Credit and Industry

ditions in the United States, where the farming carried on is very similar to that which is carried on in this county. In 1732 an attempt was made in the state of Connecticut to finance agriculture on terms that could be obtained from ordinary commercial banks, but the attempt failed. A few men got together and tried to establish a species of farmers' bank, but that attempt also was a failure, largely through the antagonistic attitude adopted by the government of the then colony, and the matter was allowed to rest. But as time went on it became more and more evident to the statesmen of that country that if they were to save their agriculture an adequate supply of credit would have to be supplied on reasonable terms.
In March, 1912, President Wilson instructed the embassies and legations of the United States in Europe to inquire into the systems as applied in different European countries, and their replies contained information of such importance that in 1913 a United States commission was appointed and sent through the countries of Europe to investigate the systems in force there. But more than that was done; the conditions pertaining to agriculture in their own country were inquired into, the farmers being heard in different places with a view of ascertaining what their credit needs were and how far the then existing system of finance supplied those needs. They also investigated the methods of the banks themselves to see how far those institutions could supply the necessary funds for agriculture. I may say that associated with that commission were a number of provincial representatives from Canada, who accompanied them and studied the conditions with them.
As a result of that investigation, in 1916, an act was passed in the United States Congress known as the Federal Farm Loan Act. I shall not go into the details of the workings of that act; the point I wish to make is that conditions were found to prevail in that country such as we find to prevail in Canada to-day; that active steps were taken to inquire into those conditions and into possible remedies; that when remedies were found they were adopted and applied. They built up a system of co-operation from the bottom, culminating, through the twelve federal banks, into a farm loan board-a system of co-operation backed in the first instance by the government itself. They took the ground we have taken right along: that the matter had ceased to be a purely agricultural matter; that it was of interest to the country as a whole that agriculture should prosper and should be able to carry on in the best pos-

sible manner; that it was a national problem that would have to be solved in a national way.
Attempts were made in Canada, with varying success, to establish provincial associations or organizations with somewhat similar ends in view. I say, with varying success, because in some provinces the attempt was successful, and in others not so much so. However, the experience derived from the efforts made in that direction points to the fact that this is a national problem rather than a provincial one and should be approached from the national point of view.
The Farm Loan Board have loaned out a great deal of money to the farmers, very largely by selling bonds, and the work has being exceedingly successful. It has assisted in the upbuilding of a great many successful and prosperous agricultural communities where before the men were, as we are in the West at the present time, discouraged and downhearted. The Farm Loan Board provided for a term of credit of about thirty-five years on the amortization plan. But this was not found to wholly fill the bill; it did not meet the situation fully, so they are bringing forward another suggestion for filling the gap between this thirty-five year term and the short term credit given by the banks with farm credits which will run from six months to five years.
It has been said, and there is a great deal of weight to be attached to the view, that we are suffering, not from a lack of credit, but from too much credit in the past, and that what we should do is to pay our debts and not be looking for further credit to be advanced to us. But one of the chief reasons for the establishment of a better system of credit amongst the farmers is to enable them to pay off their existing debts on better terms. I repeat, that is one of the chief reasons why we want a better system of credit established. It is not so much for the expansion of credit so that the farmer may purchase more land, more live stock, more machinery; we have been through that and a lot of us have learned our lesson, but it is to enable us to pay off the present encumbrances laid upon us in a better way as they become due. That is just what they do in the United States. I looked over the percentage of money borrowed in that way that was applied to different objects, and I found that thirteen per cent of the money borrowed was applied to the purchase of more land, nine per cent to buildings and improvements, two per cent to the purchase of implements and equipment, three per cent for live stock, and sixty-eight per cent for the liquidation of present indebted-

Credit and Industry
ness, and I contend that that is largely what would happen if we could establish a system along similar lines in this country. A large portion of the credit would be devoted to the object of liquidating our present encumbrances. And what would that mean? It would mean that instead of being antagonistic to the present banking system, the scheme would be of the greatest help to the banks because it would mean more money in circulation, and that people, being able to pay their debts as they became due, without pressure, w'ould be able to buy the things they require, and industry, which is now at a standstill more or less, would begin to move again.
I am making no plea that this is a universal panacea, that this by itself will place the western provinces or the agricultural industry in Canada on a proper footing. But I do claim that this is one of the ways in which the subject might be approached. It would be one of the remedies which taken together with other remedies would put us on a proper footing and enable us to play our part worthily in the shipbuilding of our nation. For that reason I would not have moved this as a resolution for the government to establish such a system. That is not my purpose at all, but I do think it is worthy of consideration as to whether we should not inquire into the possibilities of this or other methods of finance. That, I believe, is worthy of the government's consideration. If that is a practical suggestion-and it has precedent behind it, it has proved successful in other countries, then I think it- is well worth the while of the government of this country to make inquiry as to how far it might be adapted to our needs here. I think that is a very fair request.
_ As the time is getting on, I have no intention of developing this argument further. I knew when I started I had no great contribution to make to this debate. I simply wish to throw out a suggestion which might be taken in conjunction with the resolution moved by my hon. friend from Calgary East (Mr. Irvine). I find a good deal of merit in what he said, even though I cannot understand all of it. I think his statement of conditions was a fair statement, not overdrawn. His ideas of a remedy may not coincide with the ideas prevailing in this House, may not coincide altogether with the ideas in my own mind, but the resolution itself and the principle underlying it, that of obtaining information to enable us to deal intelligently with one of the most important subjects in this country, that resolution and that principle is worthy, I think, of the consideration of any body of men
m
In conclusion, I would like to say this. The farmers of this country, as I have endeavoured to point out, are not looking to the government for something for nothing. They are not looking for some special benefit which will accrue to them at the expense of the rest of the community. As far as I am concerned I would not stand for that one moment, and as far as the men who sent me here are concerned, that is far from their ideas because it has been expressed again and again. The only thing that has been urged on me by my constituents when coming here was this, that I would study conditions as I found them according to the opportunities afforded me in this House, and founding my opinion upon those conditions, speak and vote for what I believed to be for the benefit of the country as a whole, for the building up of a united and prosperous Canada. That is what they sent me here for, and that is my endeavour in this House. I believe this question of credit is one which if not at this session, at some future session will have to be most carefully studied. The time will come when its importance will be recognized on all sides of the House so that when the subject is announced for debate, the benches, instead of emptying, will fill, because we will know that it will mean a discussion of one of the greatest problems of this or any other country. I think it is reasonable, I think it is sane, that all of us should do what we can to understand conditions as they exist now throughout this country, as we do not understand them at the present time, and to understand the remedies provided in other countries, as we do not understand them at the present time, and to use the best judgment that we unitedly have to solve a problem which is advisedly one of the greatest problems of our age.

Before the debate proceeds any further on this motion, I am obliged to say that in my opinion the amendment is not properly drafted, and is not relevant to the main motion. The main motion has for its object the investigation of the basis, the function and the control of financial credit, and the relation of credit to the industrial problems. That is the one set principle in the main motion, and the amendment should be consistent with the principle involved in the main motion. What does the amendment state? First, that the bank charters be extended for twelve months subject to such amendments of the Bank Act as may be passed during the session. Now there is nothing in this which is relevant to the
Credit and Industry

main motion. The second part of the amendment, which recommends that the final revision of the Bank Act be reserved till after the report of any committee that may be appointed under this resolution, is perhaps a little more relevant to the main motion, but it does not come at its proper time. If this main motion should be adopted by the House, a parliamentary committee would be appointed, and then instructions could be given to that committee to the effect that the final revision of the Bank Act should be reserved until after its report. But, as the amendment is drafted here, it is, in my humble judgment, totally inconsistent with the principle involved in the main motion. Let me on this point read what Bourinot, in his fourth edition at page 321, says:
It is an imperative rule that every amendment must be relevant to the question on which the amendment has been proposed, and this rule has been invariably insisted upon by Canadian speakers.
Bourinot states that the English speakers have also finally adopted that rule, which was followed more closely by Canadian speakers. He goes on to say:
It is not, therefore, surprising that the latest English decisions are in accord with those of the Canadian speakers. Sir Erskine May-
That great authority.
-in later editions, however, lays it down "an imperative rule that every amendment must be relevant to the question on which the amendment is proposed."
In the present instance, I consider that the principle involved in the amendment is foreign to the principle involved in the main motion. There is only one exception to this rule. It is on the motion to go into Supply or Ways and Means where the policy of the government may be challenged. This is the only case in which there can be exceptions to the rule which I have just cited, and which is the rule recognized by all parliamentary authorities. I would, therefore, rule that this amendment is out of order and that the debate shall proceed on the main motion without any further consideration of the amendment. Of course, this does not prevent any other amendment being moved, but the present one is ruled out of order.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance) :
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have had a very
interesting discussion of a very important question. I do not rise for the purpose of opposing or discussing any of the views that have been presented by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Irvine) who moved the resolution, the hon member for Battle River (Mr. Spencer) who seconded it, and the hon member for Red Deer (Mr. Speak-

man) who has supported it in such moderate and eloquent terms. What I want to suggest is that no good purpose would be served by dividing the House upon it. No good purpose can be served by setting up another special committee for this purpose. It has been announced that, in not many days, a revision of the Bank Act will be submitted to the House, and while government bills are not always submitted to committees other than the Committee of the Whole, in this case, for good reasons, it is the intention of the government to submit the bill, as has been done on previous occasions, to the Committee on Banking and Commerce, with the fullest opportunity for considering every question that may be related to it. Almost every one of the questions that have been discussed this afternoon will arise in connection with the Bank Act, as indeed, most of the, speakers have discussed the merits of the Bank Act, and, therefore, a special committee appointed to consider this matter would not, I think, serve a good purpose. There are times and occasions when special committees are proper, but I do not think it is wise to multiply them unless for strong and particular reasons.
If the hon. member for Calgary East should succeed in having his motion pass, what will be the situation? We shall have the Bank Act, as I said, before many days; it will go to the Committee on Banking and Commerce, and that committee will be dealing with this very question from a practical standpoint. At the same time, there will be sitting in another room another committee dealing with all the theories that can be advanced on the same question. One is reminded of the small boy going to the circus where the performance takes place in two rings. He wants to watch both rings, and as a result, he comes away with a splitting headache. If we are to have two committees of this House running at the same time, dealing with the same thing, I am sure this will make for confusion.
I do not want to discuss the merits of the resolution. I know the importance of the question, especially as related to agriculture, as was stated by the hon. member for Red Deer. I believe, however, all these questions can be approached when the Bank Act is before the committee, and, therefore, I will earnestly ask my hon. friend not to insist in setting up a second committee. I am sure every object the hon. gentleman can have, can be covered by leaving the matter to come before the Committee on Banking and Commerce.

Mr. Speaker, I do not rise to object at all

Credit and Industry
to anything the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has said. I entirely agree with him that the only way we can make any useful progress in this important matter is to work all together at the same time. But I am not quite sure that everything comes within the scope of the Bank Act. To my mind, a,very important question of this whole matter of credit is the one that has been chiefly touched upon by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman). I refer to that kind of credit which, as he himself has pointed out, cannot be given by banks in such a way that agriculturists can well take advantage of it. I do not know that my hon. friend will have that included in any section of the Bank Act. I would like this understanding of the House -and I am quite sure my hon. friend will give it-that outside of the question of the banks themselves, outside of the question of any particular section in the Bank Act or any subject covered by it, that committee may also consider this question of agricultural loans and the kind of institution to put up which would be best adapted to look after them. That is something that, if it is at all practicable, ought to be considered, whether it will be something along the line of the Italian system or the American system or what. I am quite sure that most of the hon. gentlemen would fall in with my hon. friend's suggestion as long as we have that understanding.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can only say that so far as I have any opportunity of advising or assisting the Banking and Commerce Committee, my wish will be that they shall not be restricted, but shall give effect to a desire for a full discussion of the whole question. More than that, I cannot say, because the matter will be in the hands of that committee, but at all events, all practical questions involved in this resolution can be brought before the committee, and I feel that if another committee were appointed, confusion and delay would result.
Perhaps we can get to our point without any danger by simply referring this resolution to the Banking and Commerce Committee. That would cover everything.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I do not know that there is any objection to the resolution being referred to the Committee on Banking and Commerce, if the hon. gentleman will be content with that. If this will express the wish of the House, I will readily move that the resolution be referred to the Committee on Banking and Commerce.
. Mr. SPEAKER: Moved by Mr. Fielding, seconded by Mr. Graham, that the Committee on Banking and Commerce do investigate the basis, the function and the control of financial credit, and the relation of credit to the industrial problems.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I say that my motion is that the resolution of the hon. member be referred to the Committee on Banking and Commerce, not with any special instructions, but for such action as they deem best?
Amendment agreed to.
Have I the right to speak on the motion?

I thought the hon. member had adopted the reference to Committee on Banking and Commerce. However, if he wishes to speak, we will call it six o'clock.
At six o'clock the House took recess.
After Recess
The House resumed at eight o'clock.

Before replying, Mr. Speaker, I should like some information on one point. We could not hear the discussion that went on just before six o'clock and I am not quite sure now what is implied in the amendment, or whether it is indeed an amendment, that has been proposed. If I understand it, it is that the Committee on Banking and Commerce will be instructed by this House to act in the same capacity as a committee which might be appointed under this resolution. If that is correct, then I would acquiesce in that proposal; if not, the motion would have to come to a vote and there are a number of hon.' gentlemen who wish to speak on the subject.

The amendment of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) is that the resolution be referred to the Committee on Banking and Commerce, which, of course, would have full power to deal with this as with all other questions pertaining to the banking system. No particular instructions are given to that committee to deal with these matters; the power to consider them inheres in the committee.

The amendment reads:
That this motion be referred to the select standing committee on Banking and Commerce.
Then, Sir, there are other hon. gentlemen who wish to speak before I reply.

I wish that this point that has ben raised were cleared

Credit and Industry
up. I had intended to speak to the resolution, but if the purpose of the House is to refer this matter to the Committee on Banking and
Commerce with instructions to investigate the subject under consideration to-day, then I think I could postpone anything I have to say until a later occasion. There seems to be, however, still some doubt, particularly since the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Graham) has stated the purpose of the amendment. Personally, I would prefer to have that point cleared up before I speak.

I cannot make it any clearer. The Committee on Banking and Commerce will have full power to deal with everything pertaining to the banking question, and hon. gentlemen will have full opportunity to place their views before that committee.

It seems to me that a difficulty arises in connection with that proposal. If this matter were referred to that committee they might simply decline to consider it, and so dispose of it in that way. I would be very much opposed to that sort of treatment because I regard this question as one of paramount importance. The so-called practical man is very fond of airily dismissing new ideas with a wave of the hand and the assertion that they are mere theories, fads, and so forth. Now, we cannot honestly dispose of matters in that way. History shows us that many, if not all, of our established beliefs and practices were at one time assailed on the ground that they were new ideas or mere fancies, and their advocates were very frequently treated not only with levity but with cruelty. It does not do to condemn any new idea merely because it is new or because it is unpopular. Are our conditions at the present time so satisfactory that we need to make no effort to remedy evils that are claimed to exist? Perhaps, for some, conditions are satisfactory. Some may be disposed to say, let well enough alone. I do not doubt that for some, at least, in this country life is easy and pleasant and that there are no very serious problems. But for many others, and for us collectively as a nation, it is not so. It is not so for the; wage-earner who is out of a job and is enmeshed in the system as we have it. It is not so for the farmer who finds himself practically compelled to quit his business, to give up his home and to emigrate. It is not so for many of our people as individuals. And it certainly ought not to be so for us collectively. I take it that we here are supposed to consider the welfare of Canada, and I do not think that things are well enough to be let alone. Why, even such a staunch 
Conservative as Lord Milner, in a recent survey of social and industrial problems, is driven to a degree of radicalism that I think would astonish some hon. members on the government side, not to speak of those to my right. May I read one or two statements from Lord Milner's recent survey? He says in one place:
The real gravamen of the charge against our present industrial system is not that it involves an unfair distribution of the product, but that it mismanages, misdirects and therefore unduly limits production itself.
Then further on he recalls that before the war there were eleven million people in England living on the verge of starvation. He says:
It may be true that we do not produce sufficient to meet all their needs. But why don't we?
Speaking as to unemployment, he says:
We settle down to tolerate it just as we do the vagaries of the weather, and wait until the malady reaches an acute stage, whereupon we get in a flurry and suddenly improvise committees to look out for a palliative. Would it not be better to try and strike at the root of the evil, or at any rate to discover it.
In another place he expresses the following opinion:
The actual output of industry is far below what it ought to be, and the needs of the great body of the people remain unsatisfied, not because the means of satisfying them do not exist, but because they are not properly made use of. And they will never be properly made use of until the materials and instruments of production are controlled, if not actually owned, by independent and self-governing groups of producers, free to develop their several industries for their own benefit and that of the community, not for the advantage and under the dictation of persons who themselves take no part in the work.
And the Hon. Reginald McKenna, who certainly is not generally considered to be a radical, has recently discussed in a very illuminating way the whole problem of inflation and deflation as affecting British industry at the present time.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let me again draw attention to the paradox, the anomaly, the tragedy of the present situation. We have abundant resources, we have abundant labour power, and we have abundant equipment- these I think, are world conditions, and they are certainly true of Canada-we have all the powers of nature and science at our disposal, and yet in spite of all these powers and resources we have want, unemployment and misery-a creeping paralysis extending over our industrial structure. Do we confess ourselves baffled by this enigma? Is that the position we wish to take in this House?
I should like to direct your attention also, Mr. Speaker, to the tragic consequences of

Credit and Industry
price changes as we have seen them operating during the last few years-the awful consequences of inflation and deflation. Is there no way of stabilizing the purchasing power of our money? This, I think, is a legitimate question, and a wider question perhaps than any that is likely to confront us in the revision of the Bank Act, but in my judgment, for the reasons already stated, it is the most important question of all. Do we want to confess ourselves baffled and beaten by that problem also and say " Let well enough alone"?
Then let us look at conditions as they exist in this country. Reference has already been made to the statement that Canada is an immigration sieve, and I believe statistics will prove it to be true. Reference has been made also to our tremendous national debt with its staggering interest charges.
Now, I ask another question: Has credit, as understood in the resolution, no connection at all with these strange enigmas and great problems? If it has even the slightest connection, do you not think we ought to know what that connection is, do you not think we ought to know the facts so that we may be able to devise suitable remedies? When the stress of war came and ordinary methods were found inadequate we devised extraordinary measures to deal with the situation. The need was realized very keenly, and that need was met. Such extraordinary measures were adpoted not only in Canada but in practically all the belligerent countries. Special financial methods were resorted to in order to deal with the needs that arose out of war conditions.
There was a need then, and it was met. But what about now? Is there no corresponding need? I do not say that the need is identical with that which existed during the war years, but I do say that it is a very similar need, and almost equally pressing. And is it not just possible that we might meet it now if we knew more about the basis, the function and the control of credit?
I do not see that it matters very much if in some respects international action should be necessary. Canada at all events could point the way, especially as we have now the germ of an international organization in the League of Nations, through which any fruitful and suggestive ideas might be explored and extended.
I ask again, what about our experts in political economy? Are these men of no value? Is it not possible that we may get some suggestions from them which may assist us in meeting the present need? And what of
others not occupying professorial chairs in our seats of learning, but who have given intense and patient study to some of these problems, have written about them and discussed them on the public platform, are we to take no advantage of their studies? The need is great, and consequently many people have attempted to meet it by patient research, followed by suggestions and recommendations. Personally I do not know how much value there is in many of their opinions, but I think we ought to know if there is any, and it seems to me it would be well to bring some of these experts before us and get the benefit of their advice.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I believe the resolution states a real need. I have no objection to its being referred to the Committee on Banking and Commerce, providing that the committee is instructed to investigate this question. Otherwise I would be opposed to the resolution being so dealt with, because the committee might easily say, "We have enough to do without taking up this question; we will let it stand over for another year." I think we might have some expressions of opinion on a question of this importance from hon. members on the other side of the House and from those in the extreme comer opposite. So far in the course of this debate to-day contributions to it have been confined practically to members in this quarter of the Chamber. I repeat, I certainly would oppose the reference of the resolution to the Committee on Banking and Commerce unless it be accompanied by special instructions of the nature I have indicated.

Mr. Speaker, I assure you that it is with some diffidence that I rise to address the House on this question at this time. I have anxiously watched hon. members on the other side to see if any of them would enter this debate and either help it along or try to retard it, and I have looked down here to my right, but there have not been more than five or six members present in that corner at any one time, so that my attention has not been very much diverted in that direction. I must confess I am astonished that there has been no utterance from hon. members opposite on this question. Both the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) and the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) admit that the question is a vital one and that it requires investigation-but that is all. Do you not think that their attitude is a strong argument for the appointment of a special
Credit and Industry

issue of credit based on the potential capacity of the country to produce and deliver goods, that the credit should be controlled by industrial banks applying to the particular industries concerned. Then we have advocated in Nova Scotia the decentralization of the banks and the increasing of their capitalization to meet the necessity of this country for currency. We have the Australian Commonwealth bank favoured and supported by a large number of people in this country. We have the United States system of banking, with decentralization, doing away with the big monopoly, and having a string of small banks all over the country. In view of all these proposals and the support they are receiving, does not the House think the time has come for a full and impartial investigation? No banking committee would have time to go into the question of credit; that is utterly out of the question, and the Minister of Finance knows that, I am sure. What we do require is a special committee appointed for the purpose, and if it is possible, Mr. Speaker, to give that committee permission to sit through the whole year, we should do so, because no committee can sift all these proposals in a few months and arrive at a conclusion. What we want is a committee which would sit a whole year, or longer, if necessary, until a solution has been found.

It has struck'me as singular that not one member has advanced an argument in opposition to my argument for an investigation of the credit system. It is also very singular that hon. gentlemen opposite have been silent on the matter entirely. When I compare the enthusiasm with which they discussed, patronage, a paltry question, almost unworthy of being discussed on the floor of the House, with the interest they display on the great question of credit and finance, admitted by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) to be great and important, it will appear that the silence is not complimentary to hon. members on the government side of the House.
The hon. Minister of Finance offered the following objections. He said that no good purpose could be served by bringing this thing up at this time. I should like to know when the proper time- is to bring anything in here. No matter when a resolution comes from this side of the House and no matter what is proposed, the objection always is that it is the wrong time, some other time would be better. The plea of the government always is, we might possibly on some other occasion consider it, but we must not consider now.

That is becoming rather a popular though tiresome objection to proposals.
Another of his objections was that no good purpose could be gained by dividing the House. I am not anxious to divide the House. I hope the House will be unanimous in supporting this resolution.
His next objection was that a special committee would not be required seeing that there is a banking committee. The Minister of Finance knows very well that the purpose for which the banking committee exists is to deal with legislation. They will be dealing with bills, and it will take them practically all session to deal with the Bank Act revision, which is a gigantic task. The Minister of Finance knows very well that there is a distinction between the work of an investigational committee such as we desire, and the work of a select standing committee We want a committee to investigate the basis, and the function of credit and the relation of credit to the industrial paralysis that obtains in Canada at the present time. But if this parliament will instruct the select standing Committee on Banking and Commerce to act in the same capacity as the committee that we are advocating the appointment of, then there will be no objection. I believe, however, to refer this resolution to that committee in the manner proposed by the amendment is, not only not giving the resolution a decent burial, but digging a little hole for it and packing it in. If we are going to bury it, let us bury it properly, with that pomp which becomes this House.
In conclusion, let me point out what this parliament -has admitted by its silence. H I may assume that silence gives consent, then hon. members of the government side have admitted that our industrial conditions are due directly to the lack of financial credit; that Canada can use her own credit if she so desires, without going to the United States to borrow it; that those who control finances do control governments and the policies of industry; that money is not performing the original function for which it was designed; that the financial system is in danger of collapse; that a fundamental change in our credit system is required, and that there is a great need for more information. Only, they have said: "This is not the time to get information ; this is not the time for the financial system to collapse. We will ask it to collapse when we are ready for that; we will not bother about its collapsing just now. This is not the time for us to inquire into the functions of a thing that is not functioning." They have also said that this is not the time to do all the other things that they

have silently admitted to be facts. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) answers all these arguments with a little circus story; but if that little circus story in the mouth of the Minister of Finance, speaking for the government, be a sufficient answer for this government to my argument, it is not a good enough answer for me.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. A. ROBB (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the suggestion of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) that this question should be referred to the Committee on Banking and Commerce seems to me, not only reasonable, but very practical. The hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Irvine) has introduced a resolution which, all will admit, has a relation to the banking and credit of this country. Let us not forget that the Committee on Banking and Commerce is a committee of this House and a committee representing, not only supporters of the government, but all groups in this House. It is interesting to note that my hon. friend who moved the resolution is himself a member of the Banking and Commerce Committee, and that the hon. member for Brant (Mr. Good) and the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) are also members of the Banking and Commerce Committee. In short, nineteen or twenty members of the group opposite who are supporting this resolution are members of the Banking and Commerce Committee. Therefore, when the Minister of Finance suggested that we should refer this matter to the Banking and Commerce Committee, he did so with the idea, not of burying it, but of getting the best information possible before the committee specially selected under our constitution to deal with this matter. Let us assume, for a moment, that the government would accept the idea of the hon. member who moved this resolution. What would that mean? It would mean that we would be referring the question to another committee that might possibly keep the hon. member for Calgary East busy at a time when he should be before the Banking and Commerce Committee bringing out the information which members of this House all desire. Therefore, the suggestion of the Minister of Finance is with the idea, not of burying this resolution, but of getting more information and bringing it before the Banking and Commerce Committee, so that the House may be in a position to deal intelligently with the matter. If the Banking and Commerce Committee reports that it is not satisfactory, then hon. gentlemen opposite will have an opportunity to debate the question when the report of that committee is taken into consideration. The
government have but one desire, and that is to obtain the fullest information possible, so that Canada may deal intelligently with her banking and commerce laws as presented to parliament this year.

Mr. Irvine moves, seconded by Mr. Good:
That, in the opinion of this House, a representative Parliamentary committee should be appointed to investigate the basis, the function and the control of financial credit, and the relation of credit to the industrial problems.
To this Mr. Fielding moves, seconded by Mr. Graham, in amendment:
That the words:
'a representative parliamentary committee should be appointed' should be struck out, and the following substituted therefor:	'the question of appointing a
representative parliamentary committee'
And that the following words be added to the main motion:
'be referred to the standing Committee on Banking and Commerce.'
For the information of the House, I shall read the motion as it would stand, if amended:
That, in the opinion of this House, the question of appointing a representative parliamentary committee to investigate the basis, the function and the control of financial credit, and the relation of credit to the industrial problems, be referred to the standing Committee on Banking and Commerce.

Amendment agreed to.
Motion as amended, agreed to.

Whereas Eastern Galicia and Northern Bukowina were constituted on November 9. 1918, as an independent state under the name of West Ukrainian Republic ;
And whereas the integrity of this state is guaranteed by the League of Nations of which League Canada is a member; therefore be it resolved that this House urge upon the government the -desirability of making representations through its accredited representatives, to the Councils of the League of Nations, the necessity of early, complete and final settlement of the Ukrainian question.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in presenting the case in support of the resolution before the House, perhaps it is essential that I should give a brief resume of the history of the Ukraine and of the Ukrainian people in order that we may arrive at a better understanding of the question. From the dawn of history, there has been a distinct Ukrainian race with a language of its own and possessing a literature that is a thousand years old. The early history of the Ukraine is one series of bloody wars with the Poles and Lithuanians on the west, the Muscovites on the north, and the Turks and Tartars on the east. These wars
West Ukrainian Republic

gave rise to the organization of the renowned Cossacks or free warriors to defend the Ukraine against these invaders. Their early institutions appear to have been very democratic and their Hetman or President was elected by popular vote of the fighting men, and all authority lay in the hands of a general assembly whose decisions were enforced by elective officers.
In 1854, for mutual protection against the Poles on the one side and the Turks on the other, the independent Ukrainian state signed a Treaty of Union with Russia. This union gradually developed into subjugation of the state to Russia. The Cossacks were given many privileges, and became part of Russia's best fighting force. By a treaty with Poland, Russia conceded Galicia, the western part of the Ukraine, to Poland. On the dismemberment of the latter country in 1772 Galicia or west Ukraine became Austrian territory, and remained so unitl 1918. On the breaking up of that Empire, the members of the Austrian diet representing the eastern part of Galicia met and formed a national government and proclaimed the independent state of West Ukraine. This country has a population of about 6,000,000, seventy-four per cent of which is Ukrainian, about twelve per cent Poles, the balance German and Jews. It is a rich country with oil wells, forests and productive land.
Poland, remembering that this had been a part of her ancient kingdom, invaded the infant state in November 1918, and a bloody war ensued with varying success for several months. The Poles made insistent demands on the Allies for assistance in repelling the supposed Bolsheviks from East Galicia. Fearing the spread of the Bolshevik movement west, the Supreme Council of the Peace Conference consented to military occupation of the country by the Poles with the understanding that the right of self-determination was eventually to prevail. Later, the army commanded by General Haller was placed at the disposal of Poland. General Haller was a former Austrian officer and his army was composed of Poles recruited from the Allied armies, principally from the army of the United States. This army was well trained, equipped and provisioned and against it the poorly armed fighting force of the Ukrainian state made desperate but ineffectual resistance. Attacked by the Bolsheviki on the one side and by the Poles on the other, the greater part of the army was destroyed, the remnant taking refuge in Czecho-Slovakia. Since then Poland has been in control of the state and is using her military power to stamp out the national and intellectual life of the Ukrainian people. She has taken measures towards in-

corporating East Galicia into the Polish state. This action the people are fiercely resisting, and are daily coming into bloody conflict with the Polish officers. These conflicts are resulting in a destruction of life and property almost as bad as actual warfare. It is estimated that during the past season over $100,000,000 worth of grain and other farm produce has been destroyed by the peasants, rather than have it confiscated by their oppressors. Some idea of the sufferings endured by the people of this little state may be understood from the fact that it is estimated that upwards of 100,000 of its soldiers and civilians have died in Polish prisons and detention camps. I have here a mass of evidence dealing with this, but it is too lengthy to give here. I will confine myself to a quotation, not from a Ukrainian but from a Polish paper. The " Robotnik " published in Warsaw in its issue of October 16, 1919, has this to say of the conditions accorded the Ukrainian prisoners in Polish prisons and detention camps:
The conditions prevailing in the camps for war prisoners in Modlin and Brest are horrible. That at Brest is disgusting and a disgrace to the Polish State.
Then follows a long description of the living quarters and the conditions under which these men are obliged to live.
Two months ago from 50 to 100 dead were daily taken out of this camp in which about 6,000 prisoners of war were confined. When, the interned come out of the camp and stand in line to receive their rations- a veritable procession of death presents itself. All are famished and half frozen. They scramble and fight for the sparce food and the bits left over by the soldiers in the kitchen. They eat wild berries, and even grass.
Then follows a description of the rather brutal treatment meted out to the prisoners by the soldiers.
In the night they shiver with cold, since they are covered only with rags. Once they tried to light a fire in the camp, but they were chased away by the soldiers with musket butts and the fire extinguished "for fear many might be suffocated by the smoke". They are so enfeebled that they are scarcely able to walk, and give this in excuse when commanded to a more rapid gait. For this they are treated with blows from the butts of muskets, the soldiers deal these out generously, because the "men will die anyhow".
Some of them beg "make an end of it soldier, I have starved enough". In consequence of these blows many really died, they were too weak to stand them. A soldier from Posen goes about constantly with a stick, strikes at random, hitting a head here, a face there and so on; some have even had their eyes knocked out. In despair many have jumped into the river and were drowned, others cut their throats with their knives. Terrible!
Some committees were sent there by the Polish Diet, matters were to be improved. Some of the evil-doers were arrested, and when for a second time enquiries were instituted, order was quickly established. Never-

West Ukrainian Republic
theless these awful conditions continue and will grow still worse in the coming winter.
It is high time that the guilty be held responsible, it is time to expose this terrible state of affairs to the public.
By the Treaty of St. Germain September 10,
1919,	Austria surrendered all interest in East Galicia in favour of the allied governments, who by thus accepting this territory from Austria have become responsible for its final disposal, and morally liable for the protection and welfare of its people. The Supreme Council on December 8th, 1919, drew up Poland's frontier known to-day as the Curzon. line between Poland and East Galicia, confirming the fact that East Galicia is outside Polish territory. This is an indication that the action of Poland is illegal, unwarranted and immoral. In the Treaty of Sevres, June 10,
1920,	East Galicia appears as a distinct contracting party, recognized as such by the representatives of the allied governments. Again in the Treaty of Spa, July 10, 1920, between Poland and the Allies, Poland stated implicitly that East Galicia was the property of the Allies and promised to evacuate the state on the demand of the allied governments. United States Secretary of State Colby, in a note of August 10, 1920, to the Italian Ambassador and in a statement to the press on October 10, 1920, stated emphatically that Poland must be an ethnographic state and that she must accept the Curzon line as her extreme eastern boundary. He also declared that the government of the United States advised Poland to withdraw her forces from all territory lying to the east of the Curzon line. On this occasion Mr. Colby made mention of East Galicia. He expressed his regret over the fact that Poland led by Imperialism, occupied Vilna, the capital of Lithuania, in the same arbitrary and lawless manner in which she prevously had occupied East Galicia. On December 15, 1920 the Executive Committee of the League of Nations Society of London passed a resolution calling upon the British government to take action with a vew to establishing the national independence of East Galicia. Similarly on March 20,	1922 the
Council of the French League of Nations Society called upon the French government to take action. The Council of the League of Nations at its meeting February 23rd, 1921, reported to the Council of Ambassadors at Paris impressing upon them the necessity of settling the political status of East Galicia. At a meeting of the League of Nations at Geneva on September 23rd,	1921, the Hon. Mr. Doherty, one of the Canadian representatives, moved the following resolution:
That the Assembly of the League of Nations draw the attention of the Supreme Council to the desirability of determining at an early date the legal status of East Galicia.
This resolution was passed unanimously by the league. I have here the report of the Canadian delegate to the third assembly of the League of Nations whose conferences were held between the 3rd and the 30th of September, 1922. On page 4 I find the following:
At the second assembly, on the motion of a Cana. dian delegate, a resolution was adopted expressing hope of an early setlement of the question of the status of Eastern Galicia. That matter being still unsettled, Mr. Fielding moved a renewal of the expression of last year in the following terms:
"The Assembly of the League of Nations renews its wish, expressed in the resolution adopted by the second assembly on September 27, 1921, that the council of the league draw the attention of the principal allied and associated powers to the desirability of determining at an early date the status of Eastern Galicia."
I beg leave to place upon Hansard a resolution passed at a public meeting held in the city of Winnipeg in May last and which resolution deals fully with this matter. This is signed by the chairman, Rev. Dr. Gordon, the mover, Mr. J. W. Arsenych; and the seconder, Mr. W. R. Wood.
Resolution re Ukraine
Whereas, Eastern Galicia and Northern Bukowina were constituted on November 9th, 1918, as an independent state under the name of Eastern Ukrainian Republic;
Whereas, a government of this state was formed by the duly elected representatives of the population of the state and the government under presidency of Dr. Eugene Perushevich still exists-in exile:
Whereas, Poland made an aggressive war upon the Western Ukrainian Republic in order to gain possession of her rich oil-fields, forests and lands: Whereas, on June 25th, 1919, upon Polish representations, Poland was authorized by the Supreme Council of the Peace Conference to occupy Eastern Galicia by military force, the future of the territory to be decided by the Peace Conference, Rumania in the meantime occupying Northern Bukowina:
Whereas, the territory of Western Ukrainian Republic was described as an entirely separate entity by the Treaty of St. Germain (September 10th, 1919), by the settlement of Spa (July 10, 1920), by the Treaty of Sevres (August 10, 1920) and by the declaration of British government (by Mr. Harmsworth, Under-Secretry to the Minister of Foreign Affairs), ip the British House of Commons (July 6th, 1921): Whereas, the Assembly of the League of Nations September 23rd, 1921, upon Motion of the Canadian Representative, Hon. Charles D. Doherty, unanimously passed the following resolution:-
"That the Assembly of the League of Nations draw the attention of the Supreme Council to the desirability of determining at an early date the legal status of Eastern Galicia."
Whereas, up to the present date the legal status of the territory of Western Ukrainian Republic has not been determined:
Whereas, since occupation of the Western Ukrainian territory until present moment, Poland assumes right of sovereignty over this territory and exercises same: Whereas, this undertermined legal status of the Western Ukrainian Republic and Polish pretensions create abnormal conditions there; and
West Ukrainian Republic

Whereas, according to press reports, private letters and testimony of eye-witnesses arriving in Canada, the following state of affairs obtains in Galicia: Poland forces Ukrainians to accept Polish allegiance and change of religion: Poland suppresses Ukrainian language on Ukrainian territory; Polish authorities have suppressed Ukrainian public schools, high schools and higher educational institutions and do not allow to establish private schools; thousands of Ukrainian youth are deprived of educational facilities: Ukrainian lectures at the University of Lemberg are abolished; when a private Ukrainian University was established in Lemberg, its president, some professors and many students were imprisoned; practically all Ukrainian cultural, social and benevolent institutions [DOT] were crippled, hampered and ultimatily suppressed and prohibited, and Ukrainian Citizens' Relief Committee at Lemberg, which was handling the Ukrainian Red Cross moneys collected in Canada for the relief of Ukrainians, was deliberately disorganized and prevented from working by the Polish government: Ukrainian economic organizations are prevented to engage in reconstruction of the country: Ukrainian public men are being persecuted, imprisoned, slain or starved without reasonable cause: Ukrainian press is hampered, confiscated and suppressed; with the aid of military forces, a census of population was instituted by Polish authorities, and Ukrainians under pain of imprisonment. and maltreatment and heavy fines were forced to declare allegiance to Poland; Eastern Galicia is being colonized by Polish immigrants while the-Ukrainians are not alowed to buy land; Polish authorities make requisitions of grain and cattle without payments; the Polish Diet in Warsaw imposed upon Eastern Galicia an extraordinary levy of 20,000,000,000 Polish marks for the upkeep of the large Polish army of occupation; the populations of Eastern Galicia, impoverished by the continuous war of eight years' duration will be brought to utter ruin by this levy:
Now therefore be it resolved, that we the Canadian citizens in mass meeting assembled in the Convention Hall, City of Winnipeg, this 22nd day of April, 1922, hereby urge the Dominion government and Imperial British government:-
1.	To cause a searching investigation of the conditions existing in Eastern Galicia, and to see that justice is done.
2.	To see that the claims of the Ukrainian people to an independent state within their ethnographical boundaries and the political status of Eastern Galicia be finally determined.
And that copies of this resolution be forwarded to the Dominion government, with the request that the same be forwarded to the Imperial government and to the Delegation of the British Empire at the Economic Conference at Genoa.

Mover, J. W. Absenych,
