I also wish to quote briefly from an address delivered at this meeting by the Rev. Dr. Hunter:
The Ukrainians are the third largest national group in Canada. They number in this country at the lowest estimate 350,000 people. It is time the English-speaking people were getting better acquainted with them. . . People of the British races have always believed in fair play and in justice. When nearly half a million of our Canadian population are kept in distress and agitation by reports of hideous cruelty to their friends and relatives in Europe, it is a matter that concerns Canada.
And further, from the Rev. J. M. Shaver's address on the same occasion:

I am here, in the second place, because I believe that your helping your people at home does not make you less valuable Canadians but on the other hand makes you more valuable. The man who can easily forget the land which gave him his mother, his basic moral principles, his early loves and hates and hopes and fears, is a dangerous man. I am always expecting such a man to be a "crook" of some sort. It is the strongest characters who do not change so easily.
Further on Mr. Shaver states:
This brings me the expression of some reasons why you have a right to ask for our sympathy. First of all, because we know what freedom is and we know that the only way to keep our freedom is to help others to get it.
Second, because your sacrifice to save Europe from the invading Tartar and Turk was a sacrifice for us, for which we have never been able to pay.
Third, because you are largest non-English speaking group of fellow-citizens in western Canada to-day.
The occupation of East Galicia by the military forces of Poland remains in force tc the present day. But this occupation is provisional and will cease just as soon as the Supreme Council determines the political relationship of this country. In other words the ultimate international status of East Galicia remains as yet to be defined, and the duty of determining this status devolves upon the allied and associated powers or their representative body, the Supreme Council of the Peace Conference, because by article 91 of the Treaty of Saint Germain, the allied and associated powers are the sovereigns of East Galicia.
Until recently, settlers in this country from East Galicia were described on their naturalization certificates as "Citizens of Poland." During the past session, I had frequent interviews with the Under Secretary of State about this matter; and in my letter to him of June 22nd, I dealt with the legal status of these people and pointed out that in reality they were wards of the allied governments. The department, I understand, referred the subject of my letter to the British authorities, and I have here a letter from the department, which in part reads as follows:
Adverting to Mr. Mulvey's letter to you of June 22, 1922, with respect to applicants for naturalization of Ukrainian origin, I beg to inform you that this department is now describing such persons as "subjects of allied powers" and any applicants who received certificates describing them as "Poles" may have their certificates changed by returning them to this department.
The action of the under-secretary of State in this matter of naturalization is greatly appreciated by my constituents as well as by all the people of Ukrainian origin in Canada. If anything further were necessary to prove to this House that Poland has no legal status in East Galicia, it is the fact that our own Department of Secretary of State now legally

West Ukrainian Republic
describes people from that country as "subjects of the allied powers." To-day, 350,000 Canadians of Ukrainian origin beseech the Canadian parliament to hearken to the agonized appeal of 4,000,000 of their suffering and oppressed countrymen in Central Europe. Do not fail them in this the hour of their need. Show them that the great heart of the Canadian people goes out to them in this, their country's darkest hour. Tell them that the country that laid 60,000 of her best and bravest sons on the altar of sacrifice that one small country might be free, has a sympathy as deep as her mighty lakes, as wide as her noble prairies, as vast as her natural heritage; and that this appeal in the interest of justice and right shall not go unheeded by the representatives of the people of Canada.

I desire to say a few words in reference to this important resolution brought forward by the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell), who stated that it might be well for the people of Canada to cultivate the acquaintance of our Ukrainian settlers. We have in Canada to-day about 350,000 of these people who have been settled in the western part of the country for about twenty years. In that time they have developed perhaps more rapidly than any other non-English speaking class of immigrants who have come to this country. So great has been their development that today there are hundreds of their young men and women teaching English in our public schools in Manitoba. Quite a number of their women are graduate nurses, while there are several lawyers among them. You will find these people in the high schools and universities of western Canada. There are a large number of successful merchants among them carrying on business according to the standards that are recognized and pursued in this country. They also include a large body of farmers, and they are a people that lean naturally towards mixed farming. Possibly one reason for this is the fact that they produce large families and in this way provide that free labour without which mixed farming cannot be carried on in Canada. Recently they elected four of their nationality as members of the local legislature of Manitoba and these men hold their own with our own people very well. The young Ukrainian men and women who have grown up in this country in the last twenty years and who have been educated in our schools speak English as fluently and as correctly as our own people. In fact their whole record in Canada is one of which any people might be proud. Now,
it may be suggested that these people, now that they have made their homes in this country, should forget their troubles in the old land and settle down to business here. But we must remember that they have relatives back in their native country who are being persecuted and if they neglected to look after the welfare of their relatives in any part of the world, they would, I think, be neglecting one of the first duties of citizenship.
In presenting this resolution we are not asking that Canada should interfere in European questions. We are merely asking that Canada take an interest in these new Canadians and so help to make them better citizens, because I believe, Sir, that the best way to make an immigrant take an interest in his country is for the country to take an interest in him. In a word, we are merely asking the government to request the League of Nations to look fully into this question and see that justice is done in Eastern Galicia.

I do not intend to speak at length on this resolution, Mr. Speaker, because the mover (Mr. Campbell) presented the case in a manner so complete and convincing that it was apparent he had made a study of it. I had the pleasure last 3?ear in this House to defend these people when they were being ridiculed by some hon. members for wearing she'epskin coats. Now I am here to urge on the government the desirability of making representations to the League of Nations so that these Ukrainians will be freed from further oppression at the hands of the Poles. I know very well these Ukrainians who. have made their homes in western Canada, and I can endorse everything that my hon. friend from Selkirk (Mr. Bancroft) has said about their good qualities as Canadian citizens. As he stated, they generally have large families, and if we had more of these people in the prairies there would be no need for the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) to encourage child immigration from the British Isles. These people are working hard and making a success of their farms, although their land is more or less inferior in quality, but they are dogged and persevering and will stand the bumps and succeed where we would fail.
We are very proud of that British fair play which we hear so much about. Well, this is a good time to exercise it. When the friends and relatives of these citizens of Canada are being oppressed in Europe, it is the duty of the government to prove to them that we actually practise British fair play, that it is not a mere expression, but means something that can be invoked for the succour of the oppres-
West Ukrainian Republic

sed. Therefore I think this resolution should receive the unanimous support of this House and that the government should thereupon make representations to the League of Nations urging upon it the desirability and necessity of an early and final settlement of the Ukrainian boundaries, and so relieve the friends and relatives of our Ukrainian fellow citizens from the sufferings they are now enduring at the hands of Poland.

I wish to speak very briefly in suport of the resolution, Mr. Speaker. I happen to have a great many of these people in my constituency, and I can vouch for their good qualities-given a fair chance they are among the best immigrants we have and develop into very good Canadian citizens. I think we cannot do better than ask the government to bring the request of these people before the League of Nations, so that they may realize the value of their Canadian citizenship and its effectiveness in relieving the distress of their friends and relatives in the west Ukrainian Republic.

Mr. Speaker, it is a far cry from Canada to the Ukraine. However, I happen to have a certain number of Ukrainians in my constituency, and I feel great deal of interest in them for I find them to be admirable settlers who invariably develop into good Canadians.
But I am not exactly clear about the situation that is involved in this resolution. When we contemplate the troubled state of Europe and the chaotic conditions brought about by the warring and hatred that prevail there, we may be pardoned for wondering just exactly what can be done in the present situation. I have no doubt that the arrangement referred to was made by the League of Nations, and that it was agreed that the boundary line separating the new state from Poland should be definitely ascertained. But while the hon. gentlemen were discussing the resolution I had been thinking that perhaps some member of the government who understands the situation might explain it to us so that we could act intelligently. I repeat, I am not at all clear on the situation. Naturally we would all wish to see peace restored in Europe, and personally I desire to show every sympathy for the friends and relatives of our fellow citizens from the Ukraine, but until we know the situation it is difficult to act effectively. Perhaps we may get the required information from the government.

speakeroldname: Hon. W. S. FIELDING (Minister of Finance) :
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If there was any question as to the

character of these Ukrainian fellow citizens of ours in the West, I am sure we would all appreciate the information we have received from hon. members who have spoken in praise of them. I do not understand, however, that there is any such question.
I am inclined to think that the preamble of this resolution is based upon a misapprehension of one or two important points. It states that the integrity of the West Ukrainian Republic has been guaranteed by the League of Nations. I think that is a mistake. To the best of my knowledge and belief the Wes'tern Ukrainian Republic was never recognized by the League of Nations. I am afraid some of us will have to confess that our knowledge of eastern European politics is not sufficient to warrant us going very deeply into this question, but so far as we would appear to be justified in attempting to deal with it I would call my hon. friend's attention to the fact that that which he is asking to be done by this resolution has already been done. In the session of the second Assembly of 1921 the representative of Canada, the Hon. Mr. Doherty, introduced a resolution on the subject. Wisely, he did not attempt to decide the merits of the dispute. The Poles have always claimed that Eastern Galicia has been Polish for ages, and it is in their hands now under mandate. Of course, it is desirable that that condition should not remain, that the doubt should be removed and the status of Eastern Galicia determined. Mr. Doherty wisely did not attempt to say how the question should be determined, but he did say, in the name of Canada, that it should be settled. The League of Nations has no power to settle it. All the League can do is to express its opinion as to the desirability of settling this long-standing difficult question. The resolution proposed by Mr. Doherty was accepted.
At the recent sitting of the League of Nations, the third Assembly, attention was drawn to the fact that practically speaking the situation remained unchanged, Poland was still in command and the status of Eastern Galicia had not been determined. Thereupon the Canadian delegates again asked the League of Nations to re-affirm the resolution of the previous year. Mark you, Mr. Speaker, they did not undertake to settle the dispute between the Poles and the Ukrainians. They did, however, recognize that the delay was objectionable and that the matter should be settled, and thereupon a resolution was moved to renew that expression of opinion. I think my hon. friend read the resolution to which I refer, and therefore I need not read it again. Let me say that the resolution was

West Ukrainian Republic
referred to the committee for consideration, and my hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Lapointe) had the honour of being the reporter to report to the League Assembly the conclusion reached. The resolution adopted under the circumstances I have described is as follows:
The Assembly of the League of Nations renews its wish, expressed in the resolution adopted by the second Assembly on September 27th, 1921, that the council of the league draw the attention of the Principal Allied and Associated Powers to the desirability of determining at an early date the status of Eastern Galicia.
That is exactly what my hon. friend is now asking us to do. The thing which he says we should represent to the League of Nations has already been brought before that body by Canada's delegates, who moved a resolution urging that the status of Eastern Galicia should be determined, and that resolution was adopted unanimously by the League Assembly. So everything that my hon. friend is asking has been done. I think that is a clear and simple statement of the case.

Mr. Speaker, I cannot claim that there are any Ukrainians in my constituency; I do not know whether there are Ukrainians in any of the constituencies represented by this group But the late government did not' have to have the question of the wrongs of the Ukrainians brought to its notice, or the wrongs of any other nations of Europe that required assistance; these things were looked after. As the Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) points out, attention was given to them at the earliest possible moment-in 1921. I want to congratulate the hon. Minister of Finance and his colleague in following the good example that was set by his predecessors; for the present administration did what had been done before-they submitted exactly the same resolutions. I only hope that in some way or other we shall be able to get order out of tho turmoil that prevails over there now. I do not know whether the present motion will do anything to assist in that respect; as the Minister of Finance says, what is now asked has already been done. But I am quite sure that the appeals of not only the Ukrainians, but any of the other nations that found themselves in a similar position- yes, the Armenians and many others-received a ready response from the former administration.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
If any hon.
gentleman desires to speak on this subject he should do so now, because when the mover of the resolution speaks his reply will close the debate.

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the information that the Finance Minister (Mr. Fielding) has given us. I may say, however, that I was already aware of a good deal of it; in fact, most of it I have given here in speaking on the resolution. It is possible that the resolution is not quite correctly worded in its reference to the guaranteeing of the integrity of the state of West Ukraine. I understood, however, from the nature of its own constitution that the League of Nations practically guaranteed to stand for the self-determination of peoples, and that was really what I based my resolution on. I quite understand that action has been taken by the league in the matter, but I would remind hon. members about the scriptural proverb respecting the unjust judge and the poor widow. Nothing has resulted from these representations, and I would like to see some expression of opinion from this House on the matter. I appreciate and my constituents appreciate the action that has been taken by both the present and the late government in this connection. I say that I would like to have an expression of opinion from this House, but if the resolution is not in proper form of course I shall have to withdraw it. But possibly the Finance Minister could say just how it should be worded or whether I should withdraw it or not. I am quite willing to accede to his request in the matter.

speakeroldname: Hon. ERNEST LAPOINTE (Minister of Marine and Fisheries):
speechtext:
I would ask the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Campbell) to withdraw his resolution, in view of what my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) has said, and especially in view of the suggestion in the resolution that the independence of the so-called state of West Ukraine is guaranteed by the League of Nations. That state has never been recognized in fact. - The Ukrainians are asking that it should be so recognized. On the other hand, Poland asks that the Supreme Council of the Allied Powers should define what is the real status of Eastern Galicia. Both parties to the issue are asking for a settlement. Then, the final part of the resolution seems to be based on the assumption that it is for, the Council of the League of Nations to settle that question. The council cannot settle it. The Supreme Council of the Allied Powers have reserved to themselves by the Treaty of Saint Germain the right to determine and define the status of Eastern Galicia, either in the formation of an independent state or in its becoming part of Poland. The matter has not yet been determined. The result is that chaotic con-

Export of Electric Energy

ditions prevail there, and it is certainly desirable that a decision be arrived at and a settlement effected. That is what the representatives of Canada asked in 1921, as the exMinister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) has said, and that is what they asked last fall. So that Canada has already declared in favour of an early settlement by the only channel through which it can be done. I think, therefore, that the resolution should be withdrawn.

I beg leave, then, Mr. Speaker, to withdraw the resolution.
Motion withdrawn.

That, in the opinion of this House, whereas the exportation to the United States of the electric energy of the water powers of Canada, promotes the progress of the United States to the detriment of Canada, it would be desirable that the government place a prohibitive duty on this anti-national commerce.
Mr. Speaker, this question of the exportation of electrical energy, a question which is occupying the minds of our friends the Americans, is one which, for various reasons, should be immediately looked into by the government. In the first place, we cannot get a supply of anthracite coal in any part of Canada; consequently we have to import our requirements from the United States, together with a considerable quantity of bituminous coal. In other words, we have a shortage of black coal and our neighbours to the south have a shortage of "white coal". It is stated in reports of American engineers that if the present rate of domestic consumption and export of United States coal is continued, the resources now available will be completely exhausted in about forty years. Moreover, it is the policy of all countries to prohibit or restrict the exportation of material which is vital to their own welfare, being needed either for motive power, for lighting or heating, or for other uses in industry. It is not only logical, therefore, but easily understood, that the United States, finding its supply of coal becoming exhausted, will sooner or later place an embargo on exports of coal in order to conserve it for the purposes of motive power, metallurgy, lighting and heating. If this action is taken Canada will be placed in a very critical position, and the situation will be intensified if our country has allowed our neighbours to succeed in obtaining control not only of coal in the United States but electric power in Canada as well. It is in the history of all nations that a government will find the

necessary information for its administration. History will reveal the events which marked the success or failures of governments, upon which should depend the decision of all legislative bodies.
In the years 1902 and 1903 the United States felt the effects of a coal strike which brought about a scarcity of the fuel, also an inferior quality of coal, and an exorbitant increase in its cost. Our neighbours suffered in consequence, and we in Canada, as the United States acted on the principle that charity begins at home, had our supply of anthracite very much limited; in fact, the scarcity and cost were so great that coal was considered rather as a luxury, and some people lest they should forget the crisis, had particles of anthracite encrusted in their rings. At that time those who were able to procure coal at all had to pay $30 and $35 a ton. Twenty years later, that is this year, another coal strike is declared in the United States in sympathy with Canadian miners, and the same difficult conditions confront us again. We have a scarcity of coal, with poor quality and high cost. The only difference this year is that legislators are advocating in parliament and in the press that an embargo be placed upon the export of coal. Who can tell what may happen to-morrow?
These actual facts and our past experience impose upon us the duty of considering as soon as possible the whole coal problem, for the present and the future of this country will depend on the control of our white coal both as regards motive power, lighting, heating, and industry generally. Let us remember that our neighbours, who possess a considerable quantity of phosphate of lime, upon the recommendation of Mr. James R. Garfield and the late President Roosevelt, one day without warning refused to export abroad this valuable fertilizer, reserving it entirely for American territory. Remembering that according to the reports of the National Commission of Conservation in the United States their coal mines will be exhausted in forty or fifty years, and when we hear some gentlemen like Mr. George Otis Smith, director of the Geological Department of the United States, saying that it is a menace to the country to export every year forty per cent of their coal, that this raw material should be preserved to the United States for the purpose of manufacturing and supplying all the nations of the world with the goods they are in need of, we may expect before a very long time-and there is a persistent rumour to this effect-that they will impose a partial if not a total restriction on the export of American coal.

Export of Electric Energy
It is true that the central part of Canada, richly endowed as it is with white coal, could look after the situation provided that her water powers were fully worked and the exportation of our electrical energy controlled. If we export electrical energy to our neighbours to the south, it should be on the basis of a mutual exchange of white coal for black coal, so that the future and the present interests of Canada will be properly protected. Our neighbours whose commercial sense is well known, have anticipated that problem, and that is the reason why a financial group has been formed with the object of monopolizing all the American water powers so that some day they will be able to impose a price in keeping with their greed, and dictate the modus vivendi, and the American people will be compelled to accept their conditions. According to Mr. Charles Edward Wright, Assistant Attorney General at Washington, a dozen small financial groups hold one-third of all the hydraulic power of the United States, that is,
6,300,000	horse power. They have in view the time when scarcity of coal will make its use prohibitive, owing to the high price for supplying motive power, lighting and heating, thus enabling them to ask of future generations such prices as they see fit.
The following will show' in what terms exPresident Roosevelt expressed himself on this subject:
The people of our country are threatened by a monopoly more powerful than has been ever seen, as it affects very closely their domestic a'hd industrial life. Our next generation will witness a shortage of those natural resources, petroleum and gas. The price of coal will be such that hydraulic power turned into electrical energy will, owing to its cost, become the prevailing factor for transport, for manufactures, for lighting and heating our towns. Our hydraulic power alone, entirely and judiciously employed, would be adequate for the present needs of transport, industries, municipalities and private individuals. The major portion of these powers is not developed and remains the national property. It would be madness to part, without conditions, with one of our greatest resources. If we become guilty of this crime, our children will be bound to pay an annual royalty on a capitalization fixed at the highest price that the trade will stand for. They will see themselves struggling with powerful sweaters entrenched behind the doctrine of discharged rights strengthened by all means of protection that money can buy and the cunning of corporations defended by legal men. These ogres of finance will have succeeded long before then to monopolise those resources so as to be able to dictate to the people the management of their affairs and their way of existence. Public opinion will be their least worry.
Even if these monopolists of hydraulic powers and their operations are so scornfully regarded in the United States, we Canadians should take measures to nullify their calculations in regard to using, for their own benefit, hydraulic powers in Canada.
42i
The case of the Cedars rapids worked up by the Aluminium Company of America, with a plant at Massena, New York, drawing 70,000 h.p. from the flanks of the St. Lawrence, is not an example to be followed; it is antinational. We have also to guard ourselves against our own groups of Canadian financiers who are seeking to forestall the establishment of our own hydraulic powers, having in view exportation to the United States of some of the electric energy for their exclusive gain, holding up the cost of electricity to a prohibitory price, and making ready to act the same part, when opportunity arises, as the American monopolist has done.
If I am well informed, as I believe I am, the Montreal Public Service Company, now the New England Company, intend to work the rapids of Carillon by exporting to Boston
100.000	h.p. for their exclusive gain. The Electric Development Company, under their license granted by the Department of the Interior, turn into the United States at a profit
35.000	kilowatts; the Ontario Power Company,
45.000	kilowatts; the Canadian Niagara Power Company, 55,000 kilowatts; or a total of 135,000 kilowatts, or approximately 181,000 h.p. We should see at work these groups of financiers who are attempting to appropriate to themselves the powers of the Long Sault, which are second to none on the St. Lawrence. It is important that the public should be advised of the danger of allowing these to fall into the hands of these monopolists of electric powers.
Mr. Gifford Pinchot expresses himself in this manner:
Whosoever possesses the motive power is master of the industries. Have you ever seen a few drops of oil scattered on water spreading until they form a continuous layer, able to calm immediately all surface agitation? Now is the time to discuss this question and to have it known, before the various interests concentrate and forestall all the nation's property. All those that are aware of the situation admit that the time for protesting is very short. If we do not take advantage of it to protect our interests, we will hear but too late that this gathering of interests will pay little attention to the common individuals whose undertakings will be opposed to theirs.
Let us take the cost of electricity in Montreal where the consumers are charged $128 for what actually cost the company $15, prohibiting practically the use of electricity for domestic purposes. This gives an idea of the consideration these monopolists of electric powers will have in future for the consumers.
In the event of a complete shortage of anthracite in the central portion of the Dominion, we must be prepared lest our neighbours to the south take advantage of the situation with an obvious financial object in view.
Export of Electric Energy

It is our duty not to permit our hydraulic power to pass, without conditions being laid down, into the hands of wealthy individuals. In connection with this, we should highly praise the policy of the province of Ontario in hydraulic matters, its pronounced policy being to keep for the state its natural wealth. We must always remember that our friends the Americans are actually the masters of the coal, that they have in their own territory white coal in considerable quantity, although insufficient, and we must rest assured that the very day they control our hydraulic powers our national future will have disappeared.
The electric power of the Cedars is laid out to actually produce 100,000 h.p. Its capacity is 56,000 ft. per second and they propose to increase it so as to obtain 180,000 h.p. If we figure that, in 1916, the Toronto Electric Power Co. with 50,000 h.p. were supplying electric lighting and motive power to
40.000	consumers, it is clear that to provide for the wants of the Toronto Tramways, the Toronto Electric Light Co. and the Toronto Electric Power Co., the power at the Cedars would be an essential source of electric power at low cost. There is no doubt that this source of electric power at the Cedars could supply on reasonable terms the electricity to a manufacturing city of 300,000 inhabitants; in other words it could supply the motive power and lighting to 35 Canadian towns of 10,000 population and would fill about one third of the orders that are actually received by the Hydro-electric from 100- municipalities and
100.000	consumers. It is reasonable to believe that if the Aluminium Company of America had been refused electric power at the Cedars, they would have settled on Canadian territory instead of at Massena, New York.
The United States are therefore firmly convinced, and they are very much concerned over the fact, that, assuming their engineers' reports to be well founded, if they do not take possession of these water powers immediately, Canada will later acquire them under the treaty. In doing so Canada would create for herself a great number of industries which otherwise would have been established in the United States.
The Chief Engineer of the United States, Lieutenant Colonel J. C. Sanford, declares without preamble that if it is impossible to have the electric power produced in Canada passed to the American side, the American manufacturers will be drawn to Canada, where they will be able to obtain for their industries electric power at low rates. They feel already, he states, the effect of the restriction imposed on the importation of this power. The manu-
[Mr. Deolauriers.l
facturers who buy supplementary motive power in Niagara settle in Canada. Canada exports electricity from New Brunswick to the state of Maine, Quebec to New York, Ontario to the state of New York and Minnesota, British Columbia exports to the state of Washington. It is the duty of the parliament of Canada to make, for the present and future, regulations for the exportation of our electric power, essential for the welfare of the country, on a basis that will maintain with our neighbors friendly relations.
Although my resolution involves a radical embargo on the exportation of all horse-power, it does not cover all my thought. I would, though, keep to the letter of my text, if for reasons which are impossible to foresee, we could not agree without either side, the American government or the Canadian government giving way. If we take into consideration the generous way in which the Americans treated Canada when in 1902-3 a strike rendered their coal supply insufficient, it is reasonable to think that for the present and in the future Canada could exchange, on an equal basis, white coal for black coal as it has done in other natural and manufactured products, thus promoting cordial feeling and*the best interests of the two countries.
Yet I strongly share the opinion of the men I have quoted with regard to the American monopolists of hydraulic powers who, for their own personal gain, endeavour to forestall all there is of potential electric energy, as well in the United States as in Canada, with a tendency towards constituting themselves the kings of the coal and of the hydraulic powers, and sooner than we think, compelling the American and Canadian peoples to submit to their demands.
It is Canada's interest to oppose the groups of Canadian individuals who seek to forestall our water powers, taking first those which are the easiest to. develop, with a view of trading with our neighbours. They will endeavour to convert this electric power to their exclusive use, thus preventing the sale of electricity at as low a price as it is being sold at present. The result will likely be serious vexation in the future, when possibly circumstances will require the entire consolidation of all our hydraulic powers to meet the situation with regard to motive power, lighting and heating.
I believe, therefore, that it is the duty of the government to consider at once very seriously this problem of to-day and of to-morrow, and to amend and apply more vigorously than heretofore the federal act 6-7 Edward VII Chap. 16, which provides for the regulation of the exportation of electric energy and cer-

Export of Electric Energy
tain liquids and gases, and authorizes the government to impose a duty of $10 per horse power sent abroad. This is imperative unless a satisfactory agreement is reached safeguarding the present and future interests of Canada, and assisting on the scrupulous observance of the conditions and terms defined in the licenses, which are supposed to be obligatory in all cases of exportation of electric power. This would invite foreign capital and would be an incentive to the establishment of industries on Canadian soil, thus founding and developing towns like Shawinigan, Grand Mere, Three Rivers, and La Tuque.
It is only fair, however, to impose a tax on a business that pays 100 per cent profit. Such a tax would reducfe the national debt to that extent and lower the rate of taxation on the necessaries of life. It is not patriotic to allow our neighbours to acquire enormous quantities of unmanufactured pulpwood, as stressed by the Hon. Mr. Bugeaud in the Quebec House of Assembly. True it is that the practice is forbidden by a Quebec law, but Quebec cannot stop them from taking the unmanufactured pulpwood oyer the border into New Brunswick. It is, then, the duty of the federal government to impose a tax on every car of unmanufactured pulpwood, no matter what route of conveyance into foreign territory is followed. Thus we shall compel the establishment 'of the industry at home, to develop business generally and improve our means of transportation. Let us be vigilant and practise economy, and let us on every occasion show in a practical way that we love our country above all.

During the last session of parliament, when the International Joint Commission was being discussed, I opposed any joint ownership in the development of any of our water-powers. To-day, after one year's observation, I am confirmed in the view I expressed on that occasion. We in Canada to-day possess the largest amount of undeveloped hydraulic power on the American continent, and as was stated by the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Deslauriers), its value is increasing every moment. There is no doubt in the minds of those who have followed the developments in the matter of hydraulic power that there exists at the present time in the United States a powerful ring which is trying to get control of the waterpowers of the St. Lawrence The same group which fifteen years ago tried to grab that power financed the propaganda which advocated the deepening of the St. Lawrence waterways in order to gain the control of this hydraulic power. Having failed to obtain control of this power this
ring turned to the state of Maine and endeavoured to get * possession of the undeveloped water power in that state. In his-'inaugural address to the state legislature on January 5th, Governor Percival P. Baxter is reported as having said:
It is seriously urged, that the time has arrived for Maine to allow its hydro-electricity energy to be transmitted to the other New England states. Those in favor of a change in our policy say that great power developments are about to be undertaken in Canada, the purpose of which is to bring hydro-electricity from that country to Massachusetts and other New England states that are in need of it. I am told that those behind this project prefer to come to Maine and develop some of our great power locations provided they can take the power outside the state where there is a market for it, and those gentlemen say that unless this is permitted the Canadians will build their lines into New England, and once this is done Maine's power will remain idle for a long time to come.
I believe the day will come when Maine will use and need all its water power resources, and once they are taken from us, no matter how we may strive to protect the state's interests, there is grave doubt about our ever being able to recall them. If Canadian power is brought to New England the pressure that is now exerted upon our state to modify its non-transmission policy will be relieved and Maine's water powers will be left for Maine people. All the water power men of Maine are not in accord on this question and some of those who always have favoured taking power out of the state have changed their views and now believe that Maine's policy is sound.
Every word that was uttered by Governor Pereival P. Baxter applies more forcibly to the conditions in Canada to-day than they ever did. It is certain that within a short distance of the St. Lawrence in eastern Ontario and in the province of Quebec we have what is to-day the most desirable area for manufacturing that remains on the continent. There is no doubt in the minds of those who are following the tendencies of economic developments that the industries of the future are going to seek low-price hydraulic power.
Roger W. Babson in a report he lately made after a survey of the conditions in the United States has this to say about his visit to the Mohawk valley.
Every time that I visit the Mohawk valley of New York state I am more impressed with its great activity and its potential resources. I should not be surprised to see the country, lying between Albany and Buffalo, traversed by the New York, Central, the West Shore and the Erie canal, become the greatest manufacturing section of the United States. Its climate is ideal; its labour conditions are good; it abounds in agricultural resources, thus assuring a reasonable cost of living; the greatest bituminous coal mines of the country are located to the south and the greatest number of available water powers are located to the north. These conditions are certainly ideal for general manufacturing of all kinds. This valley is close not only to our great American cities, but it is well located for export trade.
Those conditions occur much more favourably on the Canadian side. Of all the waterpower that can be developed between lake
Export of Electric Energy

Mr. Speaker, I am sure the thanks of the House are due to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Deslauriers) for bringing this very important question to our notice. I do not know that it is possible for the government at the present moment to give immediate effect to the resolution, but it is perfectly clear that not only the government can, but should, see to it that no further licenses are granted for the export of electric power. We are exporting a good deal of electric power, as the hon. member has shown. It is true that this export has gone on for some considerable length of time, and it is also true that claims are set up to rights under former permits. It is also true that any rights or any permits granted by the Dominion may at any time be cancelled, and that the amount which may be exported is to be fixed each year and new application made for it.
I appreciate the troubles that a government would be in if the motion were passed in its present form. We must not forget that while we have our difficulties, our good neighbours to the south also have theirs. In that connection I noticed the other day that some gentleman in the United States said that coal shipments to Canada should be stopped. He suggested that it was idle to talk about the Canadians stopping the export of electricity, because it had been coming into the United States for so long and because so many im-

Export of Electric Energy
portant public utilities and large firms were dependent upon that source for their supply of power. Well, that is all true, but we have been getting coal from the United States much longer than the United States has been getting electricity from us, and while a great deal of inconvenience would no doubt be caused if the export of electricity from Canada to the United States was stopped, there would be great suffering in this country if no further shipments of coal were received here from the United States. We have a pretty fair modus vivendi at the present time. I do not remember the exact figures, but the amount of electricity that we export to the United States is the equivalent of a very large amount of coal. I fancy that the government should be satisfied to let things stand just about as they are, expecting that a proper supply of coal will continue to come in from the United States and on the other hand allowing a modicum of electricity to go there as at present.
But I sincerely hope the government will see to it that the amount of electricity exported is not increased. It has been shown that there is a power shortage. If we had been told a few years ago, just after the close of the war, that there was danger of a power shortage, everyone would have laughed, but I can tell the House that so marked is the present shortage *-and not only in the places referred to by the mover of the resolution-that already in Toronto they are using steam to look after their-peaks. There is already a necessity for further electrical development. I am confident that my good friend the Minister of Defence (Mr. Graham) will find in his own district a very marked shortage of power in the relatively near future. We have shortages in nearly all the different districts in Ontario from which power is supplied-*'perhaps not marked in themselves, but decidedly apparent in relation to any reasonable curve upon which the output can fairly be estimated. Unless something is done within the next two or three years it will be impossible to expand business; power will be nowhere available in the province. L urge upon the government, therefore, that no further permits be issued for the export of electricity.
The government should also consider the question of the development of water powers in the streams controlled by the Dominion. They will require no delegations to come here to tell them that that is necessary; if they will take the reports of their own officers they will see that development is required on the St. Lawrence, and that unless that development is soon made, we shall suffer severely.
Speaking generally, you cannot contract for power to-day in Ontario; there is no place in the whole Niagara district where you can at the present time arrange a firm contract for any considerable amount of power for the purposes of industry. I do not think the commission have it; I am quite sure they could not give it for any considerable length of time. There must be development in the eastern end of Ontario, with high voltages, because a voltage of 222,000 can be handled over long distances and with practically no loss.
I was surprised to hear the mover of the resolution say that the cost of power in Montreal was $128 per horse-power. Well, that is a tremendous cost; I should not have thought it was anything like that. It is true that the cost of electricity is mounting up, in the way that everything else is mounting up, but not for the same reason. The real reason is the shortage-and that in a country of infinite power possibilities. In the Niagara district you can get water power at from $17 to $45, so that I think the figure given by the hon. member is a little out of line.
The mover of the resolution stated that a company was planning to develop 100,000 horse-power in the neighbourhood of Montreal, and export it, I think he said, to Boston. I would like to know from the government whether any applications have been made for leave so to export. The Minister of Defence shakes his head. If there is any such application, Mr. Speaker, I sincerely hope that a refusal will be given. The House might well ask for a statement from the government as to its position in this matter. In the first place, is the government looking forward to a development of the power that we now have? It ought to be developed by the state; what is the government's attitude? And on the question of export, do they take the position that further amounts should be allowed to go out, or not?

ROBB (Minister of Trade and Commerce): Mr. Speaker, the resolution presented by the hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Deslauriers) and the speech he made in support of it is evidence of the fact that he is a student of this question. We all remember the veiy interesting speech he made last year on the electrification of railways. I would like to congratulate him-and I am sure it would be the wish of the House to do so-upon making such an excellent speech in the English language. I believe this is his maiden speech in the House in English.
We all recognize that the prosperity of England was due in large measure to the coal of England, and what black coal was to Eng-

land the white coal that we possess through our water-powers should be to Canada. All the provinces of Canada with perhaps one exception have some water-power and the three provinces with the largest amount .are Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia, but there is an immense amount of water-power throughout the country still undeveloped. The last speaker referred to the shortage of power that has developed, and within recent years, I gathered from his speech. That to me is an indication that there must have been a considerable development of activity in manufacturing in this country within the past few years.
The government have nothing before them to show that any person is contemplating developing immense quantities of electrical power for exportation. As was so well said by my hon. friend from West York (Sir Henry Drayton) the export of electrical power is licensed and controlled by the department, and the license must be renewed from year to year. I can assure my hon. friend the government is fully alive to the interests of Canada and if it is demonstrated that the power is required in Canada a license for its export would be very carefully considered before it was granted.
I would also point out to my hon. friend, who spoke in a rather complaining mood as if the government were giving away something they had no right to give away, that one of the first acts of the latfe government when it came into power in 1912 was to license the export of power, which my hon. friend particularly complains of to-day, from Cedar Rapids to Massena. That contract was given by the friends of my hon. friend, and this government to-day is only carrying out the contracts that we found on file when we came into office.
SIR HENRY DRAYTON: Stick to it.

In so far as it is good for the country, we will try to do that. The records show that there is no great scarcity of power in this country yet. If the power is not developed, there is ample power in this country to be developed. Water-power is not like pulp-wood or coal or some other commodity that you can store up and keep until it is required. If you do not harness water-power it simply flows on gently to the sea and is lost, so any revenue you may get from it in the meantime is revenue gained for the country. I submit that it is not sound economics to hold up the development of a product that is being wasted when it can be developed and sold at a profit to Canadians. It is questionable whether the government would be justified in placing, as some hon. gentlemen have suggested, an embargo on the export of power that might lead 
to very serious complications. Our friends to the south might say: If you are going to put an embargo on water-power, we will put an embargo on coal. Or they might put an em-embargo on some other product that was needed in this country. Embargoes are not good at any time. Control is a good thing, and so far as control is concerned, I repeat that the government will endeavour to preserve the interests of the Canadian people.
As I said in my opening remarks, what coal is to England water-power should be to Canada, and happily we have no scarcity of water-power in our country. The records show that there are still available undeveloped water-powers in Canada aggregating over 15,000,000 horse-power. The water-powers developed in Canada aggregate 2,969,659 horsepower, or about seven per cent of the total water-power available. Then as to exports, the total electrical energy exported to the United States during the calendar year 1922 was a little short of 150,000 horse-power, 149,431 to be exact.
It might interest the House to know-and this will particularly interest my hon. friend from West York, where this electrical energy is exported from-we are told that there is a shortage of electrical power in the province of Ontario, and that province rather prides itself on its control of electrical power for the use of its own people. The records show that the Ontario Power Company of Niagara Falls exported 45,000 kilowatts; the Canadian Niagara Power Company of Niagara Falls, 45,000 kilowatts; the Electrical Development Company, Limited, of Niagara Falls, 35,000 kilowatts; the International Railway Company of Niagara Falls, 200 kilowatts; the Ontario and Minnesota Power Company, Fort Frances, Ontario, 2,611 kilowatts. Last year about March the Fort Frances Company had exceeded their license, and they were rounded up by the department and compelled not to exceed the limit that was allowed to them 'under the license which we foun,d in operation when we came into office.
Sir HENRYr DRAYTON: With reference to the minister's remarks on, Ontario, which seems to be a sore subject with him, does he not know that that 45,000 kilowatts which he quite properly points out as being exported by the Ontario Power Company, was a matter of contract originally, before we had anything to do with license? Does he not also know, in connection with the Niagara Company, that before we started to license, the whole of that Niagara Company was put in with American capital with the idea of developing power for the American market?

I am not offering any observations on that, but am simply pointing out where the power is being exported from. From New Brunswick 2,500 kilowatts was exported by the Maine and New Brunswick Electric Power Company; from the province of Quebec 100 kilowatts by the Sherbrooks Railway and Power Companny; 75,000 kilowatts by the Cedar Rapids Manufacturing and Power Company, Soulanges; from British Columbia 10,000 by the Western Canada Power Company, Stave Lake; 1,500 kilowatts by the West Kootenay Power and Light Company, Ross-land; 5,000 kilowatts by the British Columbia Electrical Railway Company, Vancouver; and
28,000	kilowatts by the Bridge River Power Company of Vancouver, making a total of 44,500 kilowatts exported from British Columbia. So these three provinces, Ontario, Quebec and British Columbia, which have the largest water-powers, are also the largest exporters of power, and the largest exporter is the province of Ontario.
My hon. friend a few moments ago referred to the moving of the cotton mills from the New England states to down south because of the water-power. I am not prepared to challenge that statement. Water-power may have been the consideration, but I would point out that one of the greatest costs in the manufacture of cotton is labour, and the information I had was that the cotton mills were moving to the South because of the much cheaper labour costs there, and also because they would save the haul on the raw cotton and on part of the finished cotton down.
The hon. member for St. Mary (Mr. Des-lauriers) having presented this resolution and debated it most intelligently, having been supported by the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. Lapierre) and the hon. member for West York (Sir Henry Drayton), it seems to me that, in the best interest of the country, he might well withdraw the resolution. I imagine that he has no desire to press it to a conclusion. The government will keep before them the observations he has made; and may I repeat again, the government, always alive to the interests of this country, will see to it that the licensing of the export of electrical power will be properly controlled and the interests of the people of Canada safeguarded?

Allow me to point out to the minister that he has not answered the question I put, namely, whether the government were considering or had yet started to consider the utilization of water-powers over which they had jurisdiction. I now have in
mind the Ontario waterpowers, like the water-powers at Morrisburg, where we have a shortage. [DOT]

I should like to point out to my hon. friend that the provinces claim the right to develop water-powers, and we have no ambition to get into a controversy with our good friends from Ontario. If any person is prepared to submit a proposition to the.different departments for the development of waterpower, I am sure such a proposition will receive every consideration.
I understand, then, the question of development at Morrisburg would be entirely one for Ontario.
I did not say tl^at. So far as I know, no proposition is before the govern^ ment.
I certainly understood the minister to say that it was for Ontario.

speakeroldname: Hon. G. P. GRAHAM (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question of
power development is, of course, a live one. Any person who has read the Toronto press during the last two weeks will understand that Ontario distinctly claims the ownership of waterpowers in the St. Lawrence. Whatever the Dominion might do in the development of waterpower would be incidental. The federal authority has a right only to deal with navigation. In the Trent canal, the Trent system, the development of water-power was incidental to the improvement of navigation by deepening the canal, and a good deal of litigation took place, in which, I think, the federal authorities won out on account of the legal situation concerning much of the property along the Trent. I know I was interested in that, and our legal representatives, I think, went back a hundred years to get the title cleared of some of the properties along the Trent.
As to the St. Lawrence development, when that takes place, if it does, it will probably be of an international character, and several interests would have to be considered, first, the province of Ontario which claims ownership of the water, and, I think, with some reason. The state of New York is interested as is the province of Ontario. The federal government of the United States is interested, this being an international proposition. The federal government of Canada is likewise interested, this being an international proposition; but, as I understand the matter, whatever the federal government of Canada might do under the circumstances would be in refer-
